---

## Locality Research Guide
### Indian Territory (Present-Day Oklahoma) — Native American Tribal Records, ca. 1830–1880

---

### Jurisdictional Context

During the mid-1800s, present-day Oklahoma was **Indian Territory** — not a U.S. state or organized territory in the conventional sense. Congress designated it as a homeland for tribes removed from the Southeast under the Indian Removal Act of 1830. **Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until 1907.** This has three practical consequences for research:

- **No county-level civil records exist for this period.** No county courthouses, no civil vital registration, no standard deed books. Tribal governments and federal agencies are the record-creating authorities.
- Records created before 1907 are indexed under *Indian Territory* or individual tribe names, not Oklahoma counties. FamilySearch's volume search resolved the target period to **Indian Territory, United States**, not Oklahoma, United States.
- The **Five Civilized Tribes** — Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek (Muscogee), and Seminole — operated their own governments, courts, and record-keeping systems. Each tribe is a separate research jurisdiction with distinct records and repositories.

The **primary repositories** returned by the wiki searches are:
- **National Archives at Fort Worth, Texas** — Record Group 75 (Bureau of Indian Affairs), the single most important repository for this period
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** — holds tribal records, agency files, newspapers, and photograph collections
- **Tribal archives** — each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintains its own archive for tribal membership and citizenship records

---

### Record Classes, Availability, and Access

#### 1. Tribal Enrollment Rolls — ⭐ Start Here

**What they are:** Periodic censuses of tribal members taken by tribal governments, BIA agents, or congressional commissions. They name individuals, give ages, family relationships, and sometimes blood quantum.

**FamilySearch digitized volume found:**
| Image Group | Images | Indexed | Full-Text | Record Type | Coverage |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 002298871 | 940 | **99%** | ✅ Yes | Tribal Enrollment Cards | Indian Territory, 1840–1870 |

This volume is **name-searchable and full-text searchable** — the highest access level. It can be searched directly via FamilySearch record search.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** (Collection 1987432) — 567,890 records, 283,945 images. Date range overlaps the target period. Searchable at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)

**Specific rolls from the wiki search for the mid-1800s target window:**
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — enumerates Cherokees who removed west before the main 1838–39 removal
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — Cherokee enrollment roll compiled by John Drennen; key for identifying families in the early Indian Territory period
- Both are held at NARA Fort Worth and are partially indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry per the wiki search result (source: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records#Tribal_Rolls))

> ⚠️ **Quirk:** The Dawes Rolls (1898–1914) are the *most widely used* tribal enrollment — but they fall **outside the target period**. They are still essential: Dawes applications often include testimony about ancestors going back to the mid-1800s, making them a valuable retroactive source even when your ancestor's events occurred decades earlier. They are indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry.

---

#### 2. Annuity Payment Rolls — Annual Enumeration, 1830s–1880s

**What they are:** Bureau of Indian Affairs agents compiled annual rolls of tribal members eligible for treaty-stipulated annuity payments. They typically list heads of household and the number of family members; some include all names. These are the closest equivalent to annual census records for this period.

**Access:** Held at **NARA (Record Group 75, Microfilm M234)**. The wiki search confirmed they are **partially indexed on FamilySearch and Fold3** (source: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records#Annuity_Rolls)). Unindexed portions require browsing the M234 microfilm reel by reel.

- **FamilySearch:** Search [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) under "Indian Territory" or tribe name
- **Fold3:** [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) — subscription required; strong BIA and military collections

---

#### 3. Land Records — 1834–1907

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **"Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (Collection 1541872) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images. Covers the full target period. Searchable at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)

In Indian Territory, land was tribally held — standard U.S. land patents and county deed records do not exist for this period. Federal allotment did not begin until after the Dawes Act (1887) and the work of the Dawes Commission (1890s). Land records in this period primarily consist of **tribal land assignments and leases** recorded by tribal governments and BIA agents, not GLO patent records.

---

#### 4. Mission and Church Records — 1820–1965

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **"Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (Collection 1654321) — 123,456 records, 61,728 images. Date range covers the full target period. Searchable at [familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)

The wiki search confirmed that **Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries** established churches and schools among the relocated tribes beginning in the 1820s, maintaining registers of converts, students, baptisms, marriages, and burials. These often constitute the only vital-event record for a given family in this period.

> ⚠️ **Critical note on vital registration:** There was **no civil vital registration in Indian Territory** during the mid-1800s. Oklahoma statewide registration did not begin until after 1907 statehood. Mission registers and tribal church records are the primary (often only) source for births, marriages, and deaths in this period.

---

#### 5. Federal Census Records

Standard federal censuses for 1860 and 1870 **did enumerate Indian Territory**, though coverage was uneven — many tribal members were missed or listed under anglicized names.

- **Ancestry.com** holds the U.S. Federal Census collection (returned by the external links search) — searchable by name
- The **1860 and 1870 federal censuses** are the relevant enumerations for the target window
- **Special Indian Schedules** exist for the 1880 and 1900 censuses, naming tribal members separately with additional detail; the 1880 Special Indian Schedule for Indian Territory is an important source just outside the core target window

Access: Ancestry.com (subscription), FamilySearch (free)

---

#### 6. BIA Agency Records, Correspondence, and School Records

The Bureau of Indian Affairs maintained extensive agency records beyond annuity rolls: agent correspondence, school enrollment registers, and administrative files. These are held at **NARA Fort Worth (RG 75)** and are the backbone of the collection for this period. Some are microfilmed on M234 and partially indexed on Fold3 and FamilySearch.

**NARA online catalog:** [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) — search RG 75 for the specific tribe or agency

---

#### 7. Treaties

Treaty texts establish who was recognized as a tribal member at specific dates, what rights applied to which families, and what rolls were referenced. Treaties are at **NARA** and are fully digitized and available at [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) and through the Oklahoma Historical Society.

---

#### 8. Military Records

Some tribal members served in Indian Home Guard regiments during the Civil War (1861–65), generating pension and service records. **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) holds military records for this period and was returned as an external curated link for Oklahoma.

---

### Repositories Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA at Fort Worth, TX** | RG 75 BIA records, annuity rolls (M234), agency correspondence, tribal enrollment | Physical + partial online via Fold3 / FamilySearch |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Tribal records, photographs, newspapers, agency files | Physical (Oklahoma City) + some online |
| **Tribal archives** (each of the Five Civilized Tribes) | Tribal citizenship, membership, land, and court records | Varies by tribe; contact individually |
| **FamilySearch** | Collections 1541872, 1987432, 1654321; volume 002298871 | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses, Dawes Rolls, some BIA microfilm | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | BIA microfilm M234 (annuity rolls), military records | Subscription |

---

### Research Strategy for the Mid-1800s

1. **Identify the tribe first.** Each tribe is a separate jurisdiction. Research paths, surviving records, and repository locations differ substantially between the Cherokee Nation, Choctaw Nation, Creek Nation, Chickasaw Nation, and Seminole Nation.

2. **Work backward from the Dawes Rolls** (1898–1914) even though they're outside the target period. Dawes applications include applicant testimony and family histories reaching back to the mid-1800s, and each approved enrollee is cross-referenced to earlier rolls.

3. **Search the FamilySearch collections and the 1840–1870 volume** (002298871, 99% indexed) — this is your highest-value digitized source for the core target window.

4. **Pull annuity rolls from NARA M234** for annual snapshots of families. These are the mid-1800s equivalent of a census.

5. **Check mission registers** in FamilySearch collection 1654321 for baptisms, marriages, and deaths — the only vital records for most families in this period.

6. **Search tribal archives directly** — each of the Five Tribes has its own archive and some records are not available elsewhere.

---

### Coverage Gaps to Note

- The FamilySearch Wiki specific pages for Oklahoma Native American records, the Five Civilized Tribes, and the Dawes Roll all returned only a generic redirect via the wiki_read tool — those pages exist and are cited in the wiki search snippets, but the tool was unable to fetch their full contents. Browse them directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records) and [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Five_Civilized_Tribes_Records) for additional detail.
- The four FamilySearch Wiki place-page sections (home / getting_started / online_records / research_tips) for Oklahoma returned only generic content, not Oklahoma-specific guidance — a digitization/indexing gap in the wiki tool for this jurisdiction.
- Volume search returned only **1 digitized volume** (940 images) matching Indian Territory 1830–1880. The total FamilySearch microfilm holdings for this period in physical or undigitized form are considerably larger; the low digital volume count reflects a digitization gap, not a records gap.

---

This is a research-rich area once you know where to look — NARA Fort Worth's RG 75 holdings alone are massive. Would you like a research plan focused on a specific tribe, a specific roll series, or a particular question about an ancestor?

---

# Locality Research Guide
## Quaker (Friends) Communities — Pennsylvania, Late 1700s (~1750–1800)

### Jurisdictional Context

Pennsylvania (founded 1682 by William Penn as a Quaker refuge) had its heaviest Quaker concentrations in **Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware counties** by the late 1700s. The **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting** governed congregations across Pennsylvania and into neighboring New Jersey, Delaware, and Maryland. Pennsylvania did **not** mandate statewide civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths until **1906** — making Quaker meeting records the primary vital record substitute for this entire era.

---

### ★ Primary Record Type: Quaker Monthly Meeting Records

These are the most important records for this community and time period. Monthly meetings documented:

| Event | What It Contains |
|---|---|
| **Births** | Name, date, parents |
| **Marriages** | Names, date, location; certificates **signed by all attendees** (maps extended family & community networks) |
| **Deaths/Burials** | Name, date |
| **Certificates of Removal** | Documented a member's transfer between meetings — **critical for tracing migration** |
| **Disownments** | Members expelled for violations of Quaker discipline (e.g., serving in the Revolutionary War, marrying outside the faith); name the individual and state the cause |

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Church Records: Quaker Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Quaker_Records)*

---

### Primary Physical Repositories

**1. Friends Historical Library — Swarthmore College** (Swarthmore, PA)
The largest collection of American Quaker records in the US: manuscript monthly meeting minutes, birth/marriage/death registers, certificates of removal, and disciplinary proceedings. On-site research; finding aids via their Tripod catalogue.

**2. Quaker and Special Collections — Haverford College** (Haverford, PA)
Major complementary repository. On-site research; online catalogue available.

*Both repositories were confirmed by Wikipedia's article on Quakers in Pennsylvania.*

---

### Published Abstract: Start Here

**William Wade Hinshaw, *Encyclopedia of American Quaker Genealogy* (6 volumes)** abstracts Pennsylvania monthly meeting records and indexes individuals by name. This is the most accessible entry point before turning to original manuscripts. Available in major libraries and partially on HathiTrust and Ancestry.

*Source: FamilySearch Wiki — [Pennsylvania Church Records: Published Quaker Abstracts](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Church_Records#Published_Quaker_Abstracts)*

### Military Records (Revolutionary War, 1775–1783)

Most Quakers were **pacifists** and were expected not to serve. Those who served were often **disowned by their meeting** — making disownment minutes a genealogically significant record of the war period. For non-pacifist relatives: Revolutionary War service records and pension files are at NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) and indexed on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/).

4. **Certificates of Removal trace migration.** When a Quaker family relocated, the old meeting issued a certificate and the new meeting recorded its receipt. These documents are essential for cross-county and cross-state research.
5. **Marriage certificates list all attendees.** A Quaker marriage certificate functioned as a census of the local community — use it to identify extended kin and neighbors.
6. **Disownment records are genealogically rich.** The Revolutionary War period produced a wave of disownments for military service; these minutes name the individual and the offense.
7. **Dense Quaker counties:** Philadelphia, Chester, Bucks, and Delaware. If the county is unknown, start here.
8. **Philadelphia Yearly Meeting crossed state lines.** Families near the borders of New Jersey, Delaware, or Maryland may appear in records filed under neighboring meetings — check both sides.

---

# Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania — Locality Research Guide
**Allegheny County · Late 1800s Steel Era (c. 1870–1900)**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

**Allegheny County** was formed in **1788** from parts of Washington and Westmoreland counties. Pittsburgh, the county seat, sits at the confluence of the Allegheny, Monongahela, and Ohio rivers. The city grew explosively during the steel boom of the 1870s–1890s, attracting massive waves of immigrant labor — Irish, German, Polish, Slovak, Croatian, and Italian workers flooded the city and surrounding mill towns (Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Carnegie).

Because the county predates the target period and no boundary changes split it during 1870–1900, records in this era are held under a single jurisdiction: **Allegheny County**. There is no predecessor-county complication for this window.

> **Note on neighboring counties:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Allegheny County did not return a Neighboring Counties table in tool results, so I cannot name adjoining jurisdictions from verified data. Mill towns extended into **Westmoreland County** (east) and **Washington County** (south/southwest). If your ancestor lived near the city's edges, search those county record sets in parallel.

---

## 🏭 Occupational & Industrial Records — The Core of Pittsburgh Research

This is where Pittsburgh research diverges most sharply from a typical county guide. Several specialized repositories hold records that are rarely available elsewhere.

### Company Employment Records
Steel companies generated payroll ledgers, employment cards, accident reports, and pension files. These survive only **fragmentarily** — corporate record-keeping was inconsistent and many records were destroyed. What does survive is held primarily at:

- **Heinz History Center** (Pittsburgh) — holds industrial and immigration records from the Pittsburgh steel era. Part of the Smithsonian Affiliations network. Accessible in person; some finding aids online at [heinzhistorycenter.org](https://www.heinzhistorycenter.org).
- **Rivers of Steel National Heritage Area Archives** — preserves company records related to U.S. Steel and predecessor firms (Carnegie Steel, Homestead Works). Physical access required.

These records are **not digitized or indexed on FamilySearch**; the volume search for "Business" record types returned the same three statewide volumes as the general search, confirming no dedicated company record collections exist there. This is a physical-repository-only category.
*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Industrial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Industrial_Records))*

### State Factory Inspection Reports
Pennsylvania's Bureau of Industrial Statistics published annual factory inspection reports beginning in the 1870s. These list employers, number of workers, wages, and sometimes working conditions by mill or facility. Held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg). Not digitized; physical or microfilm access.

### Union Membership Lists
Ironworkers and steelworkers were organized through the **Amalgamated Association of Iron, Steel and Tin Workers**. Membership records (dues books, local lodge lists) are fragmentary but some survive at the **Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania** (now part of the Heinz History Center). The **Archives of Industrial Society** at the University of Pittsburgh Hillman Library also holds labor union records and is a premier repository for Pittsburgh working-class history.

### City Directories — Occupational Backbone
Pittsburgh city directories begin in **1813** and run continuously through the late 1800s. Each edition lists residents by name, address, and **occupation** — invaluable for tracking a steelworker's employment and residence year by year between census snapshots. Held at the **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** (Pennsylvania Department). Many editions have been digitized by Ancestry.com and are searchable online.
*(Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census and Naturalization](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))*

---

## Vital Records

**Allegheny County began recording births and deaths in 1870** — earlier than the statewide requirement, which did not take effect until **1906** (death certificates) and later for births. For the 1870–1900 window, county-recorded vital registrations exist but coverage is incomplete, especially for early years.

- **Marriage licenses**: Available from **1885** at the Allegheny County Courthouse.
- **Pre-1885 marriages**: Use the FamilySearch collection **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (collection [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957), 312,045 records / 156,023 images) and **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (collection [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909), 198,765 records, **images not available**).
- **County Marriages, 1885–1950**: FamilySearch collection [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) — 524,189 records, 312,045 images. **Indexed + images.** Directly covers the late-1880s–1900 target window.
- **Death certificates** (FamilySearch collection [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317)) begin **1906** — just after the target period ends, but very useful for any ancestor who survived into the early 20th century.

> **Note:** The FamilySearch Wiki page for Pennsylvania Vital Records redirected to a generic page in tool results; I cannot give the precise statewide registration mandate dates from that page. The county-level start dates above come from the Allegheny County genealogy wiki entry.

---

## Church Records

For immigrant steel workers, **church registers are often the single most important source** — they predate civil vital registration, record the whole family in one entry, and frequently preserve the exact village of origin in the old country.

Pittsburgh's ethnic parishes kept baptism, marriage, and burial registers from the **1840s onward**:

| Community | Parishes |
|-----------|----------|
| Irish & German | St. Paul Cathedral, St. Patrick's; earliest Catholic records |
| Slovak | Multiple Slovak Catholic & Lutheran parishes (Braddock, Homestead, McKeesport) |
| Polish | St. Stanislaus Kostka and others |
| Croatian | Sacred Heart of Jesus |
| Italian | St. Peter and Paul; later parishes |

The **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** holds many original registers and is accessible by appointment. The **Historical Society of Western Pennsylvania** also holds microfilmed church records.

FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church records, though specific Allegheny County parish volumes did not surface in the digitized volume search. Check FamilySearch catalog by county/locality for available microfilm that may require browsing image-by-image.

*(Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Vital and Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Vital_Records))*

---

## Census Records

Federal census records are **the chronological backbone** for tracing Pittsburgh steel workers.

| Census Year | Value for Industrial Research |
|-------------|-------------------------------|
| **1870** | Records occupation; first post-war boom census |
| **1880** | Lists occupation + employer relationship; mortality schedule (1879 deaths) |
| **1900** | Adds immigration year, years in U.S., naturalization status; month/year of birth |

All three are indexed and searchable on FamilySearch ([ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/)) and Ancestry.

The **1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed by fire** — a major gap. Substitute sources for 1890–1893 include city directories, state or local tax records, church records, and the 1890 Veterans Schedule (for Civil War veterans).

*(Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Census and Naturalization](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Census))*

---

## Naturalization & Immigration

The steel boom drew massive immigrant waves. Tracing the old-country origin is often the core research challenge.

- **Naturalization records, Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas, 1798–1930**: Held at the **National Archives at Philadelphia** (NARA Mid-Atlantic Region). Declarations of intent ("first papers") and petitions for naturalization may name the immigrant's birthplace, village, and witnesses.
- **FamilySearch digitized volume** (008120443): 351 images of Pennsylvania naturalization records, 1790–1915, **15% name-indexed** (English and German). The remaining 85% must be browsed image-by-image.
- **Pre-1906 naturalizations** could be filed in any court of record — also check federal district court records at NARA Philadelphia.
- **Passenger lists**: Indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch. Most late-1800s arrivals came through the port of **Baltimore** or **New York (Castle Garden/Ellis Island)**. Search both ports, as Pittsburgh immigrants used both routes.

*(Source: [Allegheny County, Pennsylvania Genealogy — Immigration Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Allegheny_County,_Pennsylvania_Genealogy#Immigration_Records))*

---

## Probate Records

FamilySearch collection [1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196): **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** — 893,214 records, 446,607 images. Fully covers the target window. Probate files can document family relationships, property, debts, and the names of heirs not found in vital records.

FamilySearch also has a state-level digitized volume (008120441): 1,180 images of probate records, 1683–1994, **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** — browse-only, image by image.

Original records are at the **Allegheny County Register of Wills**, Pittsburgh.

---

## Military Records

- Civil War veterans in the workforce during the 1870s–1890s: pension files (NARA, [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)) often contain detailed biographical information and family data.
- **Spanish-American War (1898)**: Service records and muster rolls at NARA.
- No FamilySearch digitized military volumes specific to Allegheny County surfaced in the volume search — check NARA and Fold3 directly.

---

## Cemetery & Death Records

- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)): searchable transcriptions and photographs from Allegheny County cemeteries.
- **Allegheny County death registrations, 1870–1905**: Held at the county or Pennsylvania State Archives; the FamilySearch volume (008120442, 674 images, 0% indexed) covers death records 1852–1968 and must be **browsed image-by-image**.

---

## Newspapers

Historical Pittsburgh newspapers (the *Pittsburgh Gazette*, *Pittsburgh Post*, *Pittsburgh Dispatch*) reported extensively on mill accidents, strikes (notably the Great Railroad Strike of 1877 and Homestead Strike of 1892), and immigrant community news. Search via:
- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com)) — subscription, broad digitized coverage
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free): [chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)
- **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** holds bound volumes and microfilm

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What's There | Access |
|-----------|-------------|--------|
| **Heinz History Center**, Pittsburgh | Industrial records, immigration files, Southwestern PA genealogy | In person; some finding aids online |
| **Rivers of Steel Archives** | Steel company records (Carnegie, U.S. Steel predecessors) | In person |
| **Univ. of Pittsburgh — Archives of Industrial Society** | Labor union records, working-class Pittsburgh | In person |
| **Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh** | City directories (1813+), local history, newspaper microfilm | In person and some digitized |
| **Catholic Diocese of Pittsburgh Archives** | Ethnic parish registers (baptism, marriage, burial) | By appointment |
| **NARA — Mid-Atlantic Region (Philadelphia)** | Naturalization records, federal court records | In person and some online via Ancestry/FamilySearch |

## Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **Vital records start 1870 at the county level** — earlier births and deaths must be traced through church registers, which are the only source for most immigrant families before 1870.
2. **The 1890 federal census is almost entirely lost** — bridge the gap with 1889–1891 city directories, church records, and tax lists.
3. **Company employment records are fragmentary and physical-only** — no digitized or indexed collection on FamilySearch. Plan a visit to the Heinz History Center or Rivers of Steel for any direct industrial documentation.
4. **Ethnic community + parish = origin village** — once you identify which parish a family attended (Slovak Catholic, Polish, Croatian, etc.), that parish's death/burial register often names the European village of origin — the key to transatlantic research.
5. **Naturalization volume on FamilySearch is only 15% indexed** — the remaining 85% requires browsing image-by-image; plan time for this.
6. **Mill-town ancestors may not have lived within Pittsburgh proper** — Homestead, Braddock, McKeesport, Carnegie, and Duquesne all had their own parishes, city directories, and local record sets. Identify the specific mill town before searching.
7. **Pre-1885 marriage records are split across multiple FamilySearch collections** (Civil Marriages 1677–1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700–1900) — search both, as coverage overlaps but is not identical.

# Locality Guide: Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania — 1793 Yellow Fever Epidemic (c. 1780–1810)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Formed:** Philadelphia County established 1682 from the original Penn land grant; the City of Philadelphia incorporated 1701 as a borough and later as a city. City and county remained legally distinct until the Act of Consolidation in 1854 (outside this period).
- **County seat / administrative center:** Philadelphia city
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Pennsylvania (Commonwealth)
- **Population during period:** Approximately 50,000 residents in the city in 1793 at the time of the epidemic (Wikipedia, "Yellow fever epidemic of 1793"). The epidemic killed roughly 5,000 — about one-tenth of the population — between August and November 1793. The `place_population` tool returned no data for this place and period.
- **Economy:** Major Atlantic port city; commerce, shipping, maritime trades, banking, printing, and skilled crafts dominated.
- **Ethnic composition:** Predominantly English and Welsh Quaker settler stock; substantial German, Scots-Irish, Irish, and English Anglican communities; a significant free Black population (several thousand by 1793).
- **Religious denominations:** Quakers (Friends), Anglican/Episcopal (Christ Church, St. Peter's, St. Paul's), Lutheran, German Reformed, Presbyterian, Methodist, Baptist, Roman Catholic, and African Methodist Episcopal (founded 1793–1794 by Richard Allen in direct response to the epidemic).
- **Key historical events:** 1793 was the year Philadelphia served as the national capital of the United States. The yellow fever epidemic (August–November 1793) killed ~5,000 people and caused mass flight from the city. Thousands who survived left Philadelphia for neighboring counties, generating records in Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, and Delaware counties as well.

---

## Boundary changes

- Philadelphia County boundaries were largely stable through the late 18th and early 19th centuries.
- **City vs. county distinction is critical:** In 1793, the incorporated city of Philadelphia occupied only a small portion of the county. Records may be filed under either the city corporation or the county government, depending on the type. The Act of Consolidation (1854) later merged them into one government — but for 1793 research, treat city and county as separate jurisdictions.
- **Neighboring counties to search:** Families who fled Philadelphia during the epidemic may have died or left records in **Bucks County** (north), **Montgomery County** (northwest), **Chester County** (west), and **Delaware County** (southwest/southeast, carved from Chester County in 1789). Always extend searches into these bordering jurisdictions.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania had **no statewide civil registration** in 1793. The FamilySearch Wiki notes statewide registration did not begin until **1906**. (FamilySearch Wiki search result: [Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).)
- **What exists for 1793:** No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for this period. Church registers and epidemic-specific records are the only vital documentation.
- **Gap note:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates on FamilySearch (collection 2255317, 1906–1968) and Death Records volume (008120442, 1852–1968) both postdate the epidemic by many decades and are not applicable here.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church burial registers (see below); Mathew Carey's published name list of the dead; the Committee of Citizens records; and probate filings.

### ⭐ Epidemic-specific records (highest priority for 1793)

These record classes are unique to the 1793 event and are the most direct sources for identifying the dead and displaced:

1. **Mathew Carey's "A Short Account of the Malignant Fever" (1793).** Carey published a list of names of those who died in the epidemic. Multiple editions survive. Held at the Historical Society of Pennsylvania (HSP) and widely available in university libraries. Also digitized through HathiTrust and Early American Imprints (Evans series). This is a **published finding aid** — not a manuscript register — but names individuals with context. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))

2. **Committee of Citizens minutes and reports.** Mayor Matthew Clarkson appointed a citizens' committee to organize relief during the epidemic. Their minutes and reports name committee members, relief recipients, and the dead. Held at the **Historical Society of Pennsylvania**. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))

3. **Bush Hill hospital records.** Bush Hill was the emergency hospital established during the epidemic. Patient and death records from this institution are held at the **Philadelphia City Archives** and **HSP**. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))

4. **Dr. Benjamin Rush's papers.** Rush treated hundreds of patients and kept detailed records and correspondence. His papers are held at the **Library Company of Philadelphia** and the **College of Physicians of Philadelphia**. Largely **physical only**.

### Church records

Church records are **the primary vital records source** for Philadelphia families in 1793. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))

Key congregations and their status:

| Congregation | Denomination | Record types | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Christ Church** | Anglican/Episcopal | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Registers published and partially indexed; HSP holds originals |
| **Gloria Dei (Old Swedes' Church)** | Lutheran/Swedish | Baptisms, marriages, burials | One of the oldest churches in America; registers transcribed and published |
| **St. Peter's Episcopal** | Episcopal | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Published registers |
| **Friends (Quaker) Monthly Meetings** | Society of Friends | Births, marriages, deaths, disownments | Haverford College Quaker & Special Collections; some on FamilySearch |
| **Mikveh Israel** | Jewish | Burial records | American Jewish Archives; Philadelphia Jewish Archives Center |
| **St. Mary's / St. Joseph's** | Roman Catholic | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Archdiocese of Philadelphia Archives |
| **Old Pine Street Presbyterian** | Presbyterian | Session records, burials | Presbyterian Historical Society, Philadelphia |
| **First German Reformed** | German Reformed | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Reformed Church archives; German-language records |
| **St. Michael's Lutheran** | Lutheran | Baptisms, marriages, burials | Lutheran Archives Center at Philadelphia |
| **African Church (Mother Bethel AME)** | African Methodist Episcopal | Burial and membership records | Mother Bethel AME Church; records document Black community heavily affected in 1793 |

- **The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania (GSP)** has compiled indexes to many Philadelphia church records — a critical finding aid. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))
- **Digitization level:** Many registers are **physical only** or exist as **transcribed publications**; some are on FamilySearch microfilm. The specific Pennsylvania Church Records volume (`SYNTH-PA-CHURCH`) returned by `collections_search` was explicitly flagged as a *synthetic test fixture* and is excluded from this guide.
- **Language:** German-language records exist for Lutheran and German Reformed congregations.

### Census records

- **1790 Federal Census** (three years before the epidemic): Covers Philadelphia County. Name-indexed and available free on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Establishes household composition just before the epidemic — useful as a baseline.
- **1800 Federal Census** (seven years after): Shows survivors and household reconstitution post-epidemic. Name-indexed.
- **No state census** existed for Pennsylvania in this period.
- **Tax records as census substitute:** Pennsylvania county tax lists (see Tax Records below) fill the intercensal gaps and can identify who was present in the city year by year.

### Probate and court records

- **Types:** Wills, letters of administration (intestate estates), inventories, guardianship filings — all generated at the county level by the Register of Wills and Orphans' Court.
- **Epidemic surge:** The 1793 epidemic generated a large spike in probate filings. Estates of epidemic victims would appear in Philadelphia County probate records for 1793–1796.
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196): 893,214 indexed records with images. Covers Philadelphia County. This is the most accessible online entry point. Free at FamilySearch.org.
- **Digitized volume:** Image group 008120441 (Probate Records, 1683–1994, 1,180 images) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Must be browsed image by image.
- **Physical originals:** Philadelphia City Archives; Register of Wills, City Hall.
- **Testate vs. intestate:** Search both wills (testate) and letters of administration (intestate) — epidemic deaths were often sudden, leaving no time to write a will.

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; land was distributed under Penn's proprietorship, not the federal rectangular survey).
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Originally under the Penn Proprietors; deeds recorded at the county level by the Recorder of Deeds. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for `Pennsylvania_Land_and_Property` resolved to a generic page — the FamilySearch Wiki does not provide Philadelphia-specific land guidance at this URL.
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages, ground rents (common in Philadelphia), tax records.
- **Access:** Philadelphia City Archives holds deed books. Some are available on Ancestry (subscription).

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:** The Revolutionary War (1775–1783) ended a decade before the epidemic; the Quasi-War with France was 1798–1800. Many Philadelphia men who died in 1793 would have been Revolutionary War veterans.
- **Record types:** Revolutionary War pension files and bounty land warrant applications are at NARA and searchable on Fold3 and Ancestry. These can establish family relationships for men who survived the war but died in the epidemic.
- **Fold3** (subscription): Military records — Fold3.com ([external_links_search result](https://www.fold3.com/))
- **NARA** (free/in-person): National Archives — [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)

### Cemetery records

- **Major burial grounds:**
  - Christ Church Burial Ground (notably where Benjamin Franklin is buried)
  - Gloria Dei churchyard
  - Friends (Quaker) burial grounds (multiple)
  - Potter's Field / Washington Square — used as a mass burial ground during the 1793 epidemic. Thousands of epidemic victims were buried here in unmarked or poorly marked graves.
  - St. Mary's Catholic Cemetery
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) lists many Philadelphia burials, but coverage of 1793 epidemic burials in Potter's Field is extremely sparse due to the nature of mass interment.
- **Physical records:** Sexton records and burial registers at individual churches and city archives; many are unpublished manuscripts.
- **⚠️ Gap:** The scale and speed of epidemic burials in 1793 means many deaths were recorded only in church registers or Committee records — not in formal cemetery sexton books.

### Newspaper records

- **Local papers in 1793:**
  - *Federal Gazette* (Philadelphia)
  - *General Advertiser* (later the *Aurora*)
  - *Pennsylvania Gazette*
  - *Pennsylvania Packet*
- **Content value:** Newspapers published lists of the dead, notices of businesses closing, relief fund announcements, and estate notices. The *Federal Gazette* in particular published daily mortality tallies during the epidemic.
- **Where held:** Historical Society of Pennsylvania; Library Company of Philadelphia; digitized through **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) — subscription required. Early American Newspapers (Readex) available through many libraries.
- **Digitization level:** Some titles digitized; many still on microfilm only at HSP and the Free Library of Philadelphia.

### Immigration/emigration records

- **Relevant port:** Philadelphia was one of the two major ports of entry on the East Coast in this era (with New York).
- **Record types:** Pre-1820 Philadelphia passenger lists are incomplete; the most systematic lists begin with the Steerage Act of 1819. For 1793, look to ship records at NARA (RG 36) and the published *Pennsylvania German Pioneers* volumes for German arrivals.
- **Naturalization records:** FamilySearch volume 008120443 (Naturalization Records, 1790–1915, 351 images, **15% name-indexed**, not full-text) covers this period. Naturalizations were filed in any court of record — Common Pleas, District Court, or Supreme Court.
- **NARA** holds pre-1820 passenger lists; some are on Ancestry.

### Tax records

- **Types:** Pennsylvania county tax lists (property and occupations); Philadelphia city ward tax lists.
- **Date range:** Survive from the colonial period through this era; annual lists exist for many Philadelphia wards in the 1790s.
- **Where held:** Pennsylvania State Archives (Harrisburg); Philadelphia City Archives; some transcribed by HSP.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists for 1792, 1793, and 1794 can show who was present before the epidemic, who disappeared (died or fled), and who returned — a powerful cross-check for the epidemic's impact on specific households.

---

---

## Records NOT online

The following relevant record classes have **no significant online presence** and require in-person or mail access:

- **Bush Hill hospital records** — Philadelphia City Archives / HSP (physical only)
- **Committee of Citizens manuscript minutes** — HSP (physical only)
- **Benjamin Rush patient papers and correspondence** — Library Company / College of Physicians (physical only)
- **Philadelphia ward tax lists, 1790s** — PA State Archives / Philadelphia City Archives (largely physical only; some transcribed by HSP)
- **Most church burial registers in manuscript** — individual church archives or HSP (physical; transcribed indexes at GSP)
- **Potter's Field / Washington Square burial records** — fragmentary; no systematic online index for 1793 epidemic burials here
- **Sexton records for individual congregations** — held at individual churches; some deposited at HSP

---

## Known record losses / gaps

- **No civil death registration in 1793.** Pennsylvania did not require statewide vital registration until 1906. Death documentation for epidemic victims depends entirely on church burial entries, the Carey list, Committee records, and probate filings.
- **Mass burial gap.** Thousands of epidemic victims buried in Potter's Field (Washington Square) were interred rapidly with minimal documentation. These individuals may appear in no surviving record other than the Carey list or newspaper mortality tallies.
- **Church register unevenness.** Not all Philadelphia congregations kept systematic registers; smaller or newer congregations may have no surviving records for 1793.
- **Pre-1820 passenger list gaps.** Arrivals at Philadelphia before the Steerage Act of 1819 are incompletely documented.

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the Mathew Carey list.** Carey's 1793 pamphlet ("A Short Account of the Malignant Fever") is the closest thing to a death register for the epidemic. It names many of the dead. Available free via HathiTrust. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793))

2. **Church burial records are the backbone.** For pre-1906 Philadelphia, church burial registers replace civil death certificates. Christ Church and Gloria Dei registers have been published and transcribed. The Genealogical Society of Pennsylvania has compiled indexes across many denominations. ([FamilySearch Wiki: Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records))

3. **Search probate records for epidemic-year estate filings.** A surge of administration filings in 1793–1795 reflects epidemic deaths. FamilySearch collection 1999196 (Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994) is the most accessible starting point; the physical index at the Philadelphia Register of Wills goes year by year.

4. **Use the 1790 and 1800 censuses as brackets.** Compare the two to identify households that shrank or vanished — consistent with epidemic death or permanent displacement.

5. **Search neighboring counties for displaced families.** Thousands fled Philadelphia in 1793 to Bucks, Montgomery, Chester, and Delaware counties. Some never returned. Those who died in exile will have records in those counties' church registers, tax lists, and probate files — not Philadelphia's.

6. **Tax lists as annual proxy census.** Philadelphia ward tax lists for 1792, 1793, and 1794 can show household-level disappearances. Cross-reference the pre- and post-epidemic lists to confirm a family's fate. Pennsylvania State Archives and Philadelphia City Archives hold these.

7. **The 1793 FamilySearch wiki search returned Philadelphia-specific content at [Philadelphia Genealogy — Yellow Fever 1793](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Yellow_Fever_1793) and [Philadelphia Genealogy — Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Philadelphia_Genealogy#Church_Records).** The broader FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Church Records, Land Records, and the Philadelphia County Genealogy page all resolved to a generic fallback page in this session — those specific wiki articles could not be read and their contents are not cited here. Visit them directly at FamilySearch.org for additional guidance.

8. **For Black families:** Richard Allen and Absalom Jones led Black Philadelphians in providing nursing care during the epidemic. Records of the African Church (later Mother Bethel AME) and the Free African Society document the free Black community of this era. These records are held at Mother Bethel AME Church, HSP, and the Philadelphia Archdiocesan Archives.

9. **The Naturalization Records volume (008120443, 1790–1915)** on FamilySearch is 15% name-indexed and covers this period — worth searching for immigrant residents who may have naturalized in Philadelphia courts around the time of the epidemic.

10. **FamilySearch catalog search:** Because `volume_search` resolved to the state level (Pennsylvania) rather than isolating Philadelphia-specific volumes, search the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/catalog) directly under *Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania* and *Philadelphia, Pennsylvania* to find microfilmed church registers, tax lists, and other collections not surfaced in the tool results here.

# Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Locality Research Guide
## Tracing Families Affected by the Great Chicago Fire (circa 1840–1890)

---

### Jurisdictional Overview

**Place:** Chicago, Cook County, Illinois, United States
**Period of focus:** c. 1840–1890 (bracketing the Great Fire of October 8–10, 1871)

Chicago was incorporated as a city in 1837 within Cook County. By 1870 its population was approximately 300,000. The Great Fire destroyed roughly **3.3 square miles** of the city, killed approximately 300 people, left over 100,000 homeless, and — critically for genealogists — burned the **Cook County Courthouse**, destroying most of the city's official pre-1871 records: deeds, birth and death registers, court records, and tax rolls. This is the defining record-loss event for Cook County research.

> **The single most important thing to know:** Almost all pre-October 1871 Cook County local records are gone. Your research strategy must pivot to **substitute sources** and **records held outside Cook County** (federal, state, denominational, and personal-paper collections).

---

### ⚠️ The Record Loss — What Was Destroyed

The Cook County Courthouse fire on October 8–10, 1871 consumed:

- County deeds and property records
- Birth and death registers (pre-1871 county-level registrations)
- Probate files and court records
- Tax rolls
- Many church registers held within the burned district

*(Source: Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire," https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Chicago_Fire; FamilySearch Wiki, "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire," https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)*

---

### Record Types, Availability, and Access

#### 1. 🔴 Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

| Sub-type | Dates | Records | Digitization | Repository |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Birth Certificates | 1871–1940 | ~1,450,000 | **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch (collection 2024189) |
| Death Records | 1871–1947 | ~980,000 | **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch (collection 1913456) |
| Marriage Records | 1871–1920 | ~620,000 | **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch (collection 1756321) |

**Critical gap:** All three FamilySearch collections begin in **1871** — no civil vital records survive for pre-fire Chicago at the county level, because they were destroyed. The FamilySearch Wiki states county-level civil registration began in Cook County from 1871; Illinois did not require **statewide** vital registration until 1916. For vital events before October 1871, church records are the primary substitute (see below).

*Access:* Cook County Clerk's Office holds the originals. FamilySearch holds digitized, name-indexed copies for the above date ranges.

---

#### 2. ⛪ Church Records — **Most Important Pre-Fire Substitute**

| Collection | Dates | Records | Digitization | Repository |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Illinois, Cook County, Chicago Church Records | 1833–1925 | ~285,000 | **Indexed + images** | FamilySearch (collection 1803978) |

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from parishes **outside the burn zone** survived the fire and are the primary source for pre-1871 vital events. Parishes re-established after the fire sometimes reconstructed records from members' personal papers.

**Key repositories for manuscript originals:**
- **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives and Records Center**: Holds Catholic parish registers. Chicago was a heavily Catholic immigrant city; this is essential for Irish, German, Polish, and Italian families.
- **Denomination-specific archives**: Chicago had large Swedish Lutheran, German Lutheran, Norwegian Lutheran, and Jewish immigrant communities. Check those denominations' own regional archives for surviving registers.

*Quirk:* Parishes within the 3.3-square-mile burn zone lost their registers; those in outlying neighborhoods (e.g., the North Side above the fire line, the South Side) often survived. Identify where your ancestor lived before assuming registers are gone.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)*

---

#### 3. 📋 Federal Census Records — **The Indispensable Pre-Fire Snapshot**

The **1870 U.S. Federal Census for Chicago survived intact** — the original schedules were held in Washington, D.C., not in Cook County, so the fire did not touch them. This is the single most important pre-fire record set.

| Census Year | Coverage | Digitization | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1850 | Cook County | Indexed + images | Ancestry.com; FamilySearch |
| 1860 | Cook County | Indexed + images | Ancestry.com; FamilySearch |
| **1870** | Chicago / Cook County | **Indexed + images** | **Survived the fire** — key pre-fire snapshot |
| 1880 | Chicago / Cook County | Indexed + images | Post-fire rebuilt city |
| 1900 | Chicago / Cook County | Indexed + images | Ancestry.com; FamilySearch |

Also check **Illinois state censuses** (1865 is the key intercensal year before the fire) for additional data points. **Mortality schedules** (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880) record deaths in the year preceding each census and can document fire-era deaths.

*Access:* Ancestry.com (U.S. Federal Census Collection), FamilySearch, and NARA.

---

#### 4. 🏠 Land and Property Records — Burnt Record Act of 1872

The destruction of Cook County's deed books was catastrophic, but the Illinois legislature responded with the **Burnt Record Act of 1872**, which required property owners to re-register their deeds. Two digitized volumes survive on FamilySearch:

| Volume | Image Group | Images | Searchability | Coverage | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed) | 009982110 | 38 | **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text) | Chicago, 1865–1871 | Must be browsed image by image |
| Post-fire Property Re-recordings | 009982111 | 112 | **Partially indexed** (41% indexed) | Chicago, 1871–1880 | Partially name-searchable |

*(Source: FamilySearch volume_search results)*

FamilySearch reports **2 total digitized volumes** for this place/period. This is a very small set — assume significant physical holdings remain undigitized.

**Key substitute for pre-fire ownership:** The **Chicago Title and Trust Company** assembled insurance and property records after the fire. Their collection is now held at the **Chicago History Museum** and is a vital resource for pre-fire property ownership.

*Quirk:* When researching land, search both the reconstructed pre-fire records (volume 009982110) and the post-1872 Burnt Record Act filings (volume 009982111) as a continuous trail — they document the same properties across the fire divide.

---

#### 5. ⚖️ Probate Records

Pre-fire probate files were destroyed with the courthouse. Post-fire probate records are held at the **Circuit Court of Cook County** and have been partially microfilmed by FamilySearch. The FamilySearch Wiki notes that FamilySearch microfilmed many post-fire Cook County records, but the specific volume and indexing status of probate holdings were not returned by the tool search — treat this as a physical/microfilm record set requiring direct inquiry.

*Access:* Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at **Northeastern Illinois University** holds Cook County records post-1871 and is a major repository for court and probate records.

---

#### 6. 🪖 Military Records — Held Federally, Unaffected by Fire

Federal military records were held in Washington, D.C., and survived. For men who served in the Civil War (1861–1865) — a very common situation for Chicago-area men of 1871 — these are excellent pre-fire biographical anchors:

- **Service and pension records**: NARA, available via Fold3 (indexed + images)
- **Draft registrations (Civil War)**: NARA / Fold3
- **Illinois adjutant general records**: Illinois State Archives (Springfield)

*Access:* Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); NARA Great Lakes Region (Chicago).

---

#### 7. 📰 Newspapers — Survivors Documenting the Fire and Its Aftermath

Historical Chicago newspapers survived and document the fire, its victims, displaced persons, and the city's reconstruction:

- **Chicago Tribune** (est. 1847): Continued publishing through and after the fire; its building survived. Reported extensively on fire losses, victim lists, and relief efforts.
- **Chicago Times**, **Chicago Inter Ocean**, and German-language papers also covered the disaster.

*Access:* **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) holds historical Chicago newspapers. The **Newberry Library** holds physical newspaper collections.

*Research tip:* Search October–December 1871 Chicago newspaper issues for lists of fire victims, relief recipients, and insurance claimants — these can substitute for destroyed vital and court records.

---

#### 8. 📖 City Directories — Survived Intact

Chicago city directories from the **1840s onward** survived the fire and are held at the **Newberry Library**. They provide annual snapshots of residents, occupations, and addresses — invaluable for placing ancestors in Chicago before and after the fire, and for tracking family mobility in the reconstruction years.

*Access:* Newberry Library (Chicago); some years digitized on Ancestry.com and Archive.org.

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy#Great_Fire)*

---

#### 9. 🧭 Immigration and Naturalization

Chicago was a major immigrant destination in the 1850s–1880s (German, Irish, Scandinavian, and later Polish and other Eastern European communities). Pre-1906 naturalization records were filed in any court of record — many Cook County court naturalizations were destroyed in the fire. **Federal alternatives:**

- **Passenger arrival lists** (NARA, via Ancestry and FamilySearch): Port of arrival records held federally, unaffected.
- **Post-fire naturalizations** in federal courts: NARA Great Lakes Region.
- **State and county naturalizations post-1871**: IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University.

---

### Key Repositories Summary

| Repository | Location | Strengths |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library** | Chicago, IL | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, newspapers, genealogy collections |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago, IL | Insurance records, Chicago Title and Trust Co. collection, photographs, personal papers |
| **IRAD — Northeastern Illinois University** | Chicago, IL | Cook County court, probate, and government records post-1871 |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Bernardin Archives** | Chicago, IL | Catholic parish registers, baptisms, marriages, burials |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Chicago, IL | Vital records from 1871 onward |
| **Illinois State Archives** | Springfield, IL | State-level records, adjutant general military records, state censuses |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region** | Chicago, IL | Federal court records, naturalizations, federal agency records |
| **FamilySearch** | Online | Microfilmed + digitized post-fire Cook County records; 4 indexed collections |
| **Ancestry.com** | Online | Census, city directories, some Cook County vital records |
| **Fold3** | Online | Military service and pension records |
| **Newspapers.com** | Online | Historical Chicago newspapers |

---

### Research Strategy: Working Around the Record Loss

**Step 1 — Anchor in the 1870 Census.** This is your most reliable pre-fire record for identifying who lived where in Chicago, with whom, and their origins.

**Step 2 — Check church records first for pre-1871 vital events.** Identify the family's denomination, determine which parish served their neighborhood, and check whether that parish was inside or outside the burn zone.

**Step 3 — Use the post-fire records as a mirror of what came before.** The Burnt Record Act re-recordings (FamilySearch volume 009982111, 41% indexed) and city directories immediately post-fire (1872–1875) often name the same individuals who lived in Chicago before, reconstructing a pre-fire picture through post-fire documentation.

Now let me establish the jurisdictional context for Louisiana in the 1700s.

Good — standardPlace is `Louisiana, United States`. Now I'll fire all survey calls in one parallel batch.

Here is your locality research guide, compiled from all tool results.

---

# Locality Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1699–1803)

## Jurisdiction overview

**La Louisiane** was an administrative district of New France, claimed by France from 1682. The colonial capital, New Orleans, was founded in 1718 and was the primary record-creating center throughout this period.

The 1700s encompass two distinct administrations, each leaving records in a different language and archive:
- **French colonial**: 1699–1762 (de facto until 1769) — records in French
- **Spanish colonial**: 1762 (treaty) / 1769 (actual control) – 1800/1803 — records in Spanish or bilingual

Civil authority was vested in the **Superior Council (Conseil Supérieur)**, which handled judicial, notarial, and land functions. The Catholic Church was the only legally recognized denomination under both French and Spanish rule; the **Code Noir** required baptism of all enslaved persons.

- **Economy:** Agriculture (indigo, tobacco, later sugar), garrison trade economy; enslaved African labor was foundational
- **Ethnic composition:** French colonists; German settlers (Côte des Allemands); Acadian refugees (1755–1785 resettlement); enslaved Africans; Spanish officials (post-1769); Indigenous peoples
- **Religion:** Roman Catholic exclusively
- **Key events:** Founding of New Orleans (1718); Natchez Massacre (1729); French cession to Spain (Treaty of Fontainebleau, 1762); Acadian deportation and resettlement (1755–1785); Spanish takeover (1769); Louisiana Purchase (1803)
- **Population data:** No FamilySearch population figures were returned for this period. Colonial census rolls (*recensements*) were taken ca. 1699, 1708, 1721, 1726, 1731, and 1766 and survive at ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) and partly at the Louisiana Historical Center.

## Boundary changes

- **1699–1762:** French colonial territory organized into military/administrative posts (*postes*) — no county subdivisions
- **1762:** France cedes territory west of the Mississippi to Spain; eastern Louisiana (including New Orleans's east bank) ceded to Britain; Spain did not establish administrative control until 1769
- **1769–1803:** Spanish colonial period; territory reorganized into districts (*partidos*); record language shifts to Spanish
- **1803:** Louisiana Purchase transfers the territory to the United States; US civil registration and court systems begin

> **No civil registration existed during this period.** All vital record-keeping was performed exclusively by the Catholic Church.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **None during this period.** Civil registration did not exist in colonial Louisiana. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Louisiana Vital Records, Church Records, Census, Land and Property, Probate, and Naming Customs were not returned as Louisiana-specific content by tools — those pages returned only a generic placeholder.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Catholic sacramental registers are the *only* systematic vital records for this era. They begin at St. Louis Cathedral in New Orleans in **1720**.

---

### Church records ⬅️ *Primary genealogical source for this era*
- **Denomination:** Roman Catholic exclusively
- **Record types:** Baptisms (including enslaved persons, mandated by the Code Noir), marriages, burials. Entries typically record name, parents' names, godparents or witnesses, and sometimes origin.
- **FamilySearch indexed collection:**
  - [*Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925*](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) (Collection 1612905) — 987,654 records, 493,827 images; covers the full colonial period from 1718
- **FamilySearch digitized browse-only volumes:**

| Image Group | Images | Coverage | Languages | Searchable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 004330991 | 264 | Sacramental registers, Archdiocese of New Orleans — Orleans Parish, 1720–1803 | French, Spanish | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, no full-text search |
| 004330992 | 149 | French colonial notarial acts / Superior Council records — Louisiana, 1699–1769 | French | **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, no full-text search |

> ⚠️ Both digitized FamilySearch volumes for this period must be browsed image by image with no name index. Records are in 18th-century French and Spanish script.

- **Physical repositories:** Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives (originals); Louisiana Historical Center (copies/duplicates); Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence (transcripts and administrative copies)

---

### Census records
- **No federal census** applies (US censuses begin 1790; Louisiana was not a US state until 1812)
- **Colonial census rolls (*recensements*):** French colonial enumerations taken ca. 1699, 1708, 1721, 1726, 1731; a Spanish census of 1766 and later ones also survive. These enumerate household members, landholdings, enslaved persons, and livestock.
- **Where held:** ANOM, Aix-en-Provence (primary); transcriptions published in secondary works (Robichaux, etc.); copies at Louisiana Historical Center and Louisiana State Archives
- **Access:** Physical / microfilm. Not name-indexed on FamilySearch for this period.

---

### Probate and court records
- **Authority:** Superior Council (French period); Cabildo / colonial courts (Spanish period)
- **Types:** Estate inventories, successions, tutorships (guardianships), civil and criminal proceedings, manumissions
- **FamilySearch collection:** [*Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984*](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) (Collection 2078341) — 456,789 records, 228,394 images; begins 1756 (late French period), continuing through Spanish and American eras
- **Where held:** Louisiana Historical Center (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) — Superior Council and Spanish colonial court records, partially digitized
- **Language:** French (pre-1769); Spanish (1769–1803)

---

### Land records
- **Survey system:** French long-lot (*arpent*) system — long, narrow strips perpendicular to waterways. Spain continued this system. This is **not** the US rectangular township-and-range system.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** French Crown (via Superior Council and Compagnie des Indes) issued concessions; Spain issued grants; after 1803 the US General Land Office confirmed pre-existing grants — documented in the *American State Papers: Public Lands* series.
- **Record types:** French concessions, Spanish land grants, notarial property contracts, marriage settlements, wills
- **Key finding from wiki_search** ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants)): French concessions and Spanish land grants are documented in *American State Papers: Public Lands* and in records at the Louisiana State Land Office; notarial archives in New Orleans (oldest continuous notarial office in North America) hold contracts, wills, marriage settlements, and property transactions from the **1730s onward**.
- **Where held:**
  - **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — notarial acts from 1730s; public access; some online finding aids
  - **Louisiana State Land Office** — Spanish and early American grants
  - *American State Papers: Public Lands* — available in print and via HathiTrust online

---

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** French and Indian War / Seven Years' War (1754–1763); Natchez campaigns (1729–1731); American Revolutionary War (Spanish Louisiana participated, 1779–1781)
- **Record types:** French colonial military muster rolls, officer records, pension records; Spanish colonial military records
- **Where held:**
  - **ANOM**, Aix-en-Provence — French colonial military
  - **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain — Spanish colonial Louisiana military (1769–1803)
  - **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/) — primarily post-1803 US military records; some colonial-adjacent materials
- **Note:** Most French and Spanish colonial military records require accessing archives in France or Spain.

---

### Cemetery records
- **Major sites:** St. Louis Cathedral churchyard (pre-1789); St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (New Orleans, est. 1789, Spanish period)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (https://www.findagrave.com/) has some entries, but 18th-century coverage is very thin
- **Physical records:** Burial registers are part of the sacramental register series (see Church Records); sexton records from this period are sparse

---

### Newspaper records
- **First Louisiana newspaper:** *Moniteur de la Louisiane* / Louisiana Gazette began 1794 — Spanish colonial period only. **No newspapers existed during the French colonial era (pre-1762).**
- **Where held:** Louisiana State Museum, Tulane University, Louisiana State Library (microfilm); Newspapers.com (https://www.newspapers.com/) for later runs
- **Content value for 1700s:** Very limited — only the final decade of the Spanish colonial period had a newspaper at all.

---

### Immigration / emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New Orleans (primary); Mobile (administered by Britain/Spain after 1763)
- **Record types:** Ship manifests for colonists from France; *engagé* (indentured servant) contracts; Acadian resettlement rosters (1755–1785)
- **Where held:** ANOM (Aix-en-Provence) for French colonial ship lists and *engagé* contracts; Louisiana Historical Center for local records; published Acadian resettlement lists (Hébert series, etc.)
- **Content note:** Passenger lists from this era are far less standardized than later US manifests. Acadian genealogies are extensively documented in specialized works and databases (Centre d'études acadiennes, Université de Moncton).

---

### Tax records
- **No US-style tax records** during the colonial period. French and Spanish administrative records include some property enumeration embedded within census rolls and notarial acts.
- **Substitute value:** Colonial *recensements* (census rolls) are the closest functional substitute, listing household composition and property.

---

### Notarial records (other)
The **New Orleans Notarial Archives** are arguably the most underutilized colonial-era genealogical source. From the 1730s forward, they hold:
- Marriage contracts (*contrats de mariage*) — often name parents and origins in France
- Wills and testaments
- Property inventories and sales
- Manumission documents (freeing of enslaved persons)
- Apprenticeship and *engagé* contracts

These records frequently supply information — especially French origins — not found anywhere in the sacramental registers.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | *Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925* (1612905; 987,654 records); *Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984* (2078341; 456,789 records); 2 browse-only digitized volumes (004330991, 004330992) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census (post-1803 only for Louisiana) | Subscription |
| Fold3 | Military records (primarily post-1803) | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery transcriptions (very thin for 1700s) | Free |
| Newspapers.com | Historical newspapers (earliest Louisiana papers from 1794) | Subscription |
| NARA (archives.gov) | Post-1803 federal and territorial records | Free (reading rooms); online varies |

> **Coverage note:** The volume_search returned a complete set of 2 digitized volumes for Louisiana covering 1700–1803 (totalResults: 2). Both are detailed above. The external_links_search returned 6 results for this period, all pointing to generic national repositories (Ancestry, FamilySearch Wiki, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) — no Louisiana-specific colonial-era external collections were returned.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records; Spanish colonial court records; sacramental register copies | In-person research room |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial acts from 1730s — contracts, wills, marriage settlements, manumissions | In-person; some online finding aids |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | Original sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from 1720 | In-person / appointment |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial admin. correspondence; census rolls; military records; ship passenger lists | In-person; partial online catalog at archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial Louisiana records (1769–1803) — administrative, military, land | In-person; PARES online catalog |
| **Louisiana State Archives**, Baton Rouge | Post-1803 state records; some colonial copies | In-person / mail request |
| **Tulane University, Howard-Tilton Library** | Manuscript collections, WPA transcriptions, published secondary works | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following are known to exist but are **not** accessible via online databases:
- Colonial French *recensements* (census rolls, 1699–1731) — at ANOM; not indexed on FamilySearch
- Spanish colonial census and administrative records (1769–1803) — at ANOM and Archivo General de Indias; not indexed online
- Full run of New Orleans Notarial Archives (1730s onward) — accessible only at the Research Center
- French colonial military muster rolls — at ANOM
- Many Superior Council court proceedings — partially at the Louisiana Historical Center; not comprehensively indexed

---

## Known record losses

- **New Orleans fires of 1788 and 1794** destroyed portions of the city, though the notarial archives survived both fires
- **Fragmentary pre-1720 coverage:** Records from the very first decade of New Orleans (1718–1720) are minimal
- **Outlying posts:** Records from Natchitoches, Pointe Coupée, Opelousas, and Attakapas are substantially less complete than New Orleans records and are scattered across multiple archives
- **Repeated hurricane and flood damage** has affected Louisiana archives over the centuries

---

## Research tips

1. **The sacramental register is your birth, marriage, and death certificate.** There was no civil registration. Always begin with FamilySearch Collection 1612905 (*Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925*) and the Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives. ([Louisiana Genealogy — French Colonial Records, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))

2. **Notarial acts are a gold mine for origins.** Marriage contracts at the New Orleans Notarial Archives frequently name parents and the home parish in France — information you will rarely find in the sacramental registers alone. ([Louisiana Land and Property — Colonial Land Grants, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Land_and_Property#Colonial_Land_Grants))

3. **The two FamilySearch digitized volumes must be browsed image by image.** Image groups 004330991 (264 images, sacramental registers 1720–1803) and 004330992 (149 images, Superior Council / notarial records 1699–1769) are **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable**. Plan to browse them page by page.

4. **Records are in 18th-century French and/or Spanish script.** Prepare to read (or engage a specialist in) period French or Spanish paleography. Abbreviations, naming customs, and handwriting styles differ significantly from modern usage.

5. **ANOM in France is indispensable.** The Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer in Aix-en-Provence holds French colonial census rolls, administrative correspondence, military records, and ship passenger lists not available in the US. For Spanish-period ancestors, the Archivo General de Indias in Seville is the equivalent. Both have online catalog portals.

6. **Enslaved persons appear in the sacramental registers.** The Code Noir mandated Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons. These baptismal entries may name the enslaver, sometimes note the enslaved person's African origins, and occasionally record parents' names — making them valuable for both African-American and slaveholder family research.

7. **Use WPA transcriptions and published abstracts.** The WPA in the 1930s transcribed many colonial Louisiana records. Albert Robichaux (*Colonial Settlers on the Mississippi River*), Glenn Conrad, and the Louisiana Genealogical and Historical Society have published abstracts of Superior Council records, notarial acts, and sacramental registers — far more searchable than the originals.

8. **Acadian ancestry requires specialized resources.** If your ancestor arrived as part of the Acadian resettlement (1755–1785), consult the *Dictionnaire généalogique des familles acadiennes* and the Centre d'études acadiennes databases (Université de Moncton, Canada) alongside Louisiana sources.

9. **Watch for *dit* names and name variants.** French colonial families frequently used multiple given names and *dit* (alias/called) names. A man named Jean-Baptiste could appear as "Baptiste" in one record and "Jean" in another. The *dit* name often functioned as a hereditary surname alternative. ([Louisiana Genealogy, FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy#French_Colonial_Records))

10. **Note the jurisdictional transition of 1769.** Records from 1762–1769 are in a transitional zone — the Treaty of Fontainebleau transferred Louisiana to Spain, but Spanish administration didn't begin until 1769. Records from these years may still be in French and under the Superior Council, not yet Spanish administrative forms. If your search straddles this date, check both French and Spanish record series.

---
