# Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns — Locality Research Guide
## Late 1800s (c. 1860–1905)

---

## Jurisdictional Overview

Pennsylvania's coalfields divide into two geographic zones:

**Anthracite region (northeastern PA):** Schuylkill County (formed 1811), Carbon County (formed 1843), Luzerne County, Northumberland County, and **Lackawanna County — carved from Luzerne County in 1878**. The Wikipedia Coal Region article ([en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coal_Region)) identifies these five counties as the core anthracite zone, drawing large immigrant waves from Ireland, Wales, Germany, Poland, Lithuania, Slovakia, Italy, and Ukraine from the 1820s through 1900.

**Bituminous region (southwestern PA):** Westmoreland County (formed 1773) and Fayette County are the principal counties. *Note: `place_search` did not return a distinct result for Fayette County — verify its holdings directly at FamilySearch.*

> ⚠️ **Critical jurisdictional split:** Any event in Scranton, Carbondale, or the Lackawanna Valley **before 1878** was recorded under **Luzerne County**. Always search Luzerne County records before that date for ancestors in what is now Lackawanna County.

---

## Record Types, Availability, and Access

### 1. Vital Records
The FamilySearch Wiki's Pennsylvania Vital Records page and all four Pennsylvania `wiki_place_page` sections returned only generic content — Pennsylvania-specific registration dates were not returned by these tools. The generic content notes that "many U.S. states did not require statewide registration until the early 1900s."

What the **`collections_search`** confirms is actually available on FamilySearch:

| Collection | FamilySearch ID | Dates | Records | Images |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania County Marriages | [1921317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921317) | 1885–1950 | 524,189 | 312,045 |
| Pennsylvania Civil Marriages | [1571957](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1571957) | 1677–1950 | 312,045 | 156,023 |
| Pennsylvania Compiled Marriages | [1502909](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1502909) | 1700–1900 | 198,765 | *(none)* |
| Pennsylvania Death Certificates | [2255317](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2255317) | **1906–1968** | 4,218,763 | 4,218,763 |

**Gap:** No statewide FamilySearch indexed collection for **births or deaths during the 1860s–1890s** was returned by `collections_search`. Death Certificates begin in 1906 — postdating most of this window. **Church records (see §3) are the primary substitute for vital events during this period.**

---

### 2. Census Records
Federal decennial censuses survive for **1860, 1870, 1880, and 1900** for Pennsylvania. The FamilySearch wiki_search result ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)) confirms: *"Federal census schedules (1870–1900) list occupation as 'miner' and can identify mining families."* Ancestry.com (returned by `external_links_search`) indexes the full census series.

> ⚠️ **1890 census gap:** The 1890 federal census was largely destroyed. The 1880 and 1900 censuses bracket this gap; mine employment and industrial records (§4) may substitute.

The **1880 census Manufacturers/Industry Schedules** listed mine workers by establishment and are available for some Pennsylvania counties — useful when your ancestor worked a specific colliery.

---

### 3. Church Records — HIGHEST PRIORITY FOR THIS REGION

The FamilySearch wiki_search ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)) is explicit: church registers are *"essential — ethnic parishes… served specific mining communities and their registers often contain the most detailed family data."*

Ethnic denominations present in coalfield towns:

| Wave | Community | Denominations |
|---|---|---|
| Early (1840s–1860s) | Irish | Roman Catholic |
| Early (1840s–1870s) | Welsh | Congregational, Baptist, Methodist |
| Mid (1860s–1880s) | German | Lutheran, Reformed, Catholic |
| Later (1875–1905) | Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian | Roman Catholic |
| Later (1880s–1905) | Ukrainian | Greek Catholic, Orthodox |
| Later (1880s–1905) | Italian | Roman Catholic |

**Where to search:** Local parish archives, FamilySearch microfilm holdings (check the FamilySearch Catalog by county), and diocesan archives (Diocese of Scranton, Diocese of Allentown, Diocese of Pittsburgh for respective regions). The Historical Society of Schuylkill County (Pottsville) and the Anthracite Heritage Museum (Scranton) also preserve local church materials per the Wikipedia Coal Region article.

---

### 4. Mining-Specific Records — Unique to This Region

These records exist nowhere else and can substitute for missing vital registration.

#### FamilySearch Digitized Volumes
`volume_search` returned **23 total digitized volumes** for the coalfield counties. The first page of 3 is detailed below; 20 more are behind the next-page token and await further review:

| Image Group | Coverage | Record Type | Digitization Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| [002240015](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=002240015) | Schuylkill Co., 1870–1900 | Mine Worker Employment Cards | ✅ **Indexed + full-text** (95% indexed) |
| [002240016](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=002240016) | Luzerne Co., 1870–1895 | Mine Accident Reports | 🔍 **Browse-only** (0% indexed, no full-text) |
| [002240017](https://www.familysearch.org/search/image/index?owc=002240017) | Lackawanna Co., 1878–1900 | Colliery Payroll Ledgers | 🔍 **Browse-only** (0% indexed, no full-text) |

The **browse-only** volumes must be navigated image by image — there is no name search.

#### Pennsylvania Mine Inspector Reports (1870 onward)
The FamilySearch wiki_search result ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Coal_Mining)) states these annual reports **"list fatal accidents with names, ages, nationalities, and cause of death"** — a remarkable record type for the era. The Wikipedia Coal Region article confirms they are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives** from 1870 forward.

#### Union Records
The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA, founded 1890) left **membership rolls and grievance files**, noted in the wiki_search result ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)). Covers the post-1890 period only.

---

### 5. Immigration and Naturalization
The FamilySearch wiki_search result ([Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Occupational_Records#Mining_Community_Sources)) states:
- *"Many miners immigrated through the ports of Philadelphia and New York and naturalized in county courts near the mines."*
- **"Schuylkill County naturalization records (1840s–1906) are at the Pennsylvania State Archives."**

Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record — county Courts of Common Pleas being the most common. After 1906, federal courts consolidated naturalization. **Passenger lists** for Philadelphia and New York arrivals are on Ancestry.com (returned by `external_links_search`) and indexed on FamilySearch.

---

### 6. Probate and Land Records
FamilySearch has **Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683–1994** ([collection 1999196](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1999196), 893,214 records with images) — fully covering this period and available via name search. Land deeds are held at county courthouses; miner families in company towns often rented rather than owned, so deed records may be sparse for laborers.

---

### 7. Military Records
**Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) was returned by `external_links_search` for military records, and **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) for federal archives. Civil War service records (1861–65), pension files, and Spanish-American War (1898) records are at NARA. Pennsylvania adjutant general records are at the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### 8. Newspapers
**Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) was returned by `external_links_search`. Coal towns sustained active local papers — accident reports, obituaries, and social columns regularly named miners by name, colliery, and ethnic community long before statewide death registration.

---

### 9. Cemetery Records
**Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) was returned by `external_links_search`. Ethnic and denominational cemeteries — often maintained by specific immigrant parishes or fraternal societies — are scattered throughout mining communities.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg | Mine Inspector reports (1870+), Schuylkill Co. naturalizations (1840s–1906), state collections | Wiki search result |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**, Pottsville | Local mining community records | Wikipedia Coal Region article |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum**, Scranton | Lackawanna/Luzerne mining community records | Wikipedia Coal Region article |
| **FamilySearch** | 23+ digitized volumes; marriage, probate, death collections | `collections_search`, `volume_search` |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, immigration, vital records | `external_links_search` |
| **NARA** | Federal immigration, military | `external_links_search` |
| **Fold3** | Military records | `external_links_search` |
| **County courthouses** | Deeds, probate, local court naturalizations | General |

---

## Research Quirks and Gotchas

1. **Lackawanna pre-1878 = Luzerne:** Events in Scranton, Carbondale, and the Lackawanna Valley before 1878 are filed under Luzerne County — search there first.
2. **No statewide birth/death registration in most of this window:** Pennsylvania Death Certificates begin 1906. Church baptism and burial registers are the de facto vital record system for the 1860s–1890s.
3. **Ethnic parish identity is a prerequisite:** You need to know which denomination served your ancestor's community before you can find the right church register — an Irish Catholic family and a Polish Catholic family in the same mining patch used entirely different parish books.
4. **Mine Inspector reports begin 1870:** Annual lists of fatal accidents with names, ages, and nationalities are a unique resource with no civilian counterpart — essential for miners who died on the job.
5. **20 more FamilySearch volumes not yet reviewed:** `volume_search` found 23 total digitized volumes but returned only 3 on the first page. Additional volumes for this region remain to be browsed.
6. **1890 census destroyed:** Employment records, payroll ledgers, and the 1880/1900 federal censuses must bridge this decade.
7. **Company town records are fragmentary:** Mine company employment and payroll records survive unevenly — the Pennsylvania State Archives and local historical societies hold what survives; there is no comprehensive index.

---

*FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania (all 4 `wiki_place_page` sections) and the county-specific Genealogy pages returned only generic content through these tools — researchers should consult them directly at [familysearch.org/wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/wiki) for Pennsylvania-specific registration dates and county-level research tips.*

output.text_response:
Here is the locality guide compiled from all tool results.

---

# Massachusetts Locality Guide: Early Puritan Settlements, c. 1620–1700

## Jurisdictional Context

Massachusetts in the early 1600s comprised **two legally distinct colonies** — each with its own record series:

- **Plymouth Colony (1620–1691):** Established by the Mayflower settlers; governed the Plymouth, Barnstable, and Bristol counties region. Its records are published and indexed *separately* from Massachusetts Bay Colony records. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

- **Massachusetts Bay Colony (1628–1691):** Centered on Boston; Governor John Winthrop's Great Migration brought approximately 20,000 settlers between 1630 and 1640. The colony mandated towns to record births, marriages, and deaths starting in **1639** — one of the earliest civil registration requirements in North America. ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massachusetts_Bay_Colony))

- **Province of Massachusetts Bay (1691+):** Plymouth Colony was absorbed in 1691 under a new royal charter, uniting both under one provincial government.

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** If your family lived in Plymouth, Barnstable, or Bristol counties before 1691, their records fall under **Plymouth Colony**, not Massachusetts Bay Colony. Search both jurisdictions when the family's pre-1691 location is uncertain.

---

## Record Types & Availability

### 1. 📋 Town Vital Records — *Best Online Starting Point*

**What exists:** Birth, marriage, and death records mandated at the **town level** from 1639. Some towns began recording earlier. Registration was a town obligation — not county or statewide — so compliance varies; some towns have gaps.

**FamilySearch (indexed + images):** [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) — Collection 2061550; searchable by name.

**Published compilations:** The *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series (Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for **over 200 Massachusetts towns** — an essential compiled source. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

**Repositories:** Town clerk offices; Massachusetts Archives; NEHGS; FamilySearch.

---

### 2. ⛪ Church Records (Congregational/Puritan) — *Critical Substitute and Supplement*

**What exists:** As the established church of the colony, Congregational meetings kept registers of members, baptisms, marriages, and disciplinary actions (excommunications, admonishments). Many have been published in Colonial Society of Massachusetts series and local historical society publications. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))

**FamilySearch (indexed + images):** [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) — Collection 1921657; searchable by name.

**Digitized volume — full-text searchable (not name-indexed):**
- **Image Group 007612045** — 121 images; Suffolk County, MA; 1630–1700; Congregational church admissions and baptisms. Reachable via FamilySearch full-text search; cannot search by name directly.

**Repositories:** Congregational Library & Archives, Boston (major denominational archive); individual church archives; Massachusetts Archives; FamilySearch.

---

### 3. 🗺️ Land Records

**What exists:** Deeds were recorded at the **county level** from the 1630s and survive in remarkably complete runs at county registries of deeds. Town proprietors' records document original land grants within each town. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy))

**Digitized volume — browse-only:**
- **Image Group 007612044** — 188 images; Massachusetts; 1620–1698; town meeting and proprietors' records. **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image by image with no search capability.

**Repositories:** County Registries of Deeds (deed books from 1630s); Massachusetts Archives (colony-era land grants).

---

### 4. ⚖️ Probate Records

**What exists:** Probate courts operated from the 1630s, producing wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, and letters of administration.

**FamilySearch (indexed + images):** [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) — Collection 1678901; searchable by name.

**Repositories:** County probate courts; Massachusetts Archives.

---

### 5. 🏛️ Colonial Court Records

**What exists:** The Massachusetts General Court (the colonial legislature and highest court) generated extensive records from the 1620s onward — judicial proceedings, petitions, legislative acts, and correspondence. The **Massachusetts Archives** holds the original colony records and governor's correspondence from the 1620s. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

**Largely physical/published:** Many records appear in published series such as *Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay* (Nathaniel Shurtleff, ed., 1853–1854).

**Repositories:** Massachusetts Archives, Boston; Massachusetts Historical Society.

---

### 6. ⛵ Passenger & Migration Records (Arriving Families)

**What exists — and what does NOT:** The FamilySearch collection [Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) begins in **1820 and does not cover 1600s arrivals** at all. For Great Migration arrivals (1620–1643), use these compiled sources instead:

- **Great Migration Study Series** (NEHGS, Robert Charles Anderson et al.) — documents every known settler arriving 1620–1643; searchable at [AmericanAncestors.org](https://www.americanancestors.org). ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- John Camden Hotten, *Original Lists of Persons of Quality* (1874)
- Charles Edward Banks, *Planters of the Commonwealth* (1930)

**Repositories:** NEHGS, Boston.

---

### 7. 📜 Tax & Colony Assessment Records

**What exists:** Colony tax lists and assessments placed individuals in specific towns and provide household wealth estimates — a vital substitute for census records in this era. No federal census exists before 1790; no colonial census equivalent was conducted.

**Repositories:** Massachusetts Archives; some records published in *Collections of the Massachusetts Historical Society*.

---

### 8. ⚔️ Military (Colonial Militia)

**What exists:** Colonial militia muster rolls and related records, particularly relevant for King Philip's War (1675–1676) and other colonial conflicts. Coverage on [Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/) for 1600s Massachusetts is limited; Massachusetts Archives holds the primary holdings.

---

### 9. 🪦 Cemetery Records

Many 17th-century Massachusetts gravestones survive. [Find A Grave](https://www.findagrave.com/) includes transcriptions from early New England burial grounds. Local historical societies have published extensive gravestone transcriptions.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | Colony records, General Court files, court records, governor's correspondence from 1620s | In-person; some digitized |
| **NEHGS, Boston** (AmericanAncestors.org) | Great Migration series; manuscript collections; published genealogies; *NEHGR* journal | Membership; online; research room |
| **FamilySearch** | 3 indexed collections (Vital, Church, Probate); 2 digitized volumes for 1600–1700 | Free at FamilySearch.org |
| **Congregational Library & Archives, Boston** | Congregational church registers | In-person; some digitized |
| **County Registries of Deeds** | Deed books from the 1630s (county level) | County courthouse; some digitized |
| **Massachusetts Historical Society, Boston** | Published record series; manuscript collections | In-person; some online |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Federal records post-1776; limited colonial-era material | NARA.gov |

---

## Digitization Level Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Status | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Town Vital Records 1620–1890 | ✅ Indexed + images (Collection 2061550) | Best online starting point |
| Church Records 1630–1920 | ✅ Indexed + images (Collection 1921657) | + Full-text volume 007612045 for Suffolk Co. 1630–1700 |
| Probate Records 1635–1991 | ✅ Indexed + images (Collection 1678901) | County-level |
| Town Meeting/Proprietors' Records | ⚠️ Browse-only (Volume 007612044, 188 images) | No index; browse image by image |
| Passenger Lists | ❌ FamilySearch starts 1820 | Use Great Migration series for 1620–1643 arrivals |
| Colonial Court Records | ⚠️ Largely physical / published books | Massachusetts Archives; published series |
| Tax Lists | ⚠️ Largely physical | Massachusetts Archives |
| Land Deeds | ⚠️ County Registries (physical/partial digitization) | Earliest county deed books from 1630s |

---

## Research Quirks to Know

1. **Plymouth vs. Bay Colony split (before 1691):** Always determine which colony your ancestor belonged to — Plymouth Colony records are a separate research trail.
2. **No census before 1790:** Substitute with tax lists, church membership rolls, town proprietors' lists, court records, and the Great Migration series.
3. **Search by town, not county:** Town-level vital registration means the town is the key jurisdictional unit — knowing the specific town is essential.
4. **FamilySearch coverage for 1600–1700 is narrow:** Only 2 digitized volumes were found for this exact period. The indexed collections reach back into the 1600s, but published compilations (Tanner–Corbin, Great Migration) are equally essential.
5. **Church records = vital records backup:** When town vital records are missing or sparse, Congregational church baptism/marriage registers are the primary alternative — many are published or held at the Congregational Library & Archives.
6. **FamilySearch wiki place pages** for Massachusetts returned only generic content in this session. Visit [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy) directly for the latest research guidance.

---

The **Great Migration Study Series** from NEHGS and the **Massachusetts Town Vital Records collection** on FamilySearch are the two most powerful starting points for early Puritan settler families. From there, layer in church records, probate, and land deeds to build out full family profiles.

# Oklahoma, Land Run Era (1889–1910) — Locality Research Guide

---

## Jurisdictional Context

The Land Run of 1889 opened the **Unassigned Lands** of present-day central Oklahoma to non-Native settlement on April 22, 1889. An estimated 50,000 participants raced to stake homestead claims; land offices at **Guthrie** and **Kingfisher** processed applications under the General Land Office (GLO).

On **May 2, 1890**, Congress passed the Organic Act, formally creating **Oklahoma Territory** with Guthrie as capital. The territory organized 26 counties between 1890 and 1907.

**Critical jurisdictional split to understand from the start:** Throughout 1889–1907, Oklahoma Territory and **Indian Territory** coexisted as two separate federal jurisdictions covering adjacent parts of present-day Oklahoma. Records for non-Native settlers generally fall under Oklahoma Territory; records for citizens of the Five Civilized Tribes, freedmen, and intermarried whites living in Indian Territory fall under **Indian Territory** and its governing body, the Dawes Commission (active 1893–1906). Which jurisdiction applies to a given ancestor depends on their legal status, not simply where they lived geographically. Search both before concluding a record does not exist.

On **November 16, 1907**, Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged to form the **State of Oklahoma**.

Records created before county organization (mostly 1889–early 1890s) were filed at the territorial level. County formation was rapid but uneven — always identify which county held jurisdiction for a given township on the date of the event you are researching.

---

## 🏆 Priority Records for This Era

### 1. Land Records — START HERE
**Digitization: Indexed + Images (partial)**

Land and homestead records are the single most important record class for Land Run research. Every settler who filed a claim generated a paper trail.

**FamilySearch Collection:**
- [Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images. Covers homestead applications, final certificates, and patents for both Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory.

**Digitized Volume on FamilySearch:**
- Image Group **005221388** — Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs, 1889–1907. 402 images, **74% name-indexed** (searchable by name via record_search). Includes original applications, settlement proof narratives with witness names, and final patents. *Rejected applications also survive and may contain family details.*

**Bureau of Land Management GLO Records (free):**
- [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) — Searchable index of land patents issued through the GLO (Record Group 49). Free to search; downloadable patent images.

**National Archives — Washington, D.C.:**
- Record Group 49, General Land Office. Full homestead case files (applications through final proof) are held here. Files often include affidavits of neighbors as witnesses, which can reveal the claimant's age, origins, and family situation. *These are among the richest biographical records for Land Run families.*

> **Quirk:** Homestead proof required five years of continuous residence and improvement before a patent was issued. A settler who proved up in 1894 will have a 1889 application *and* a 1894 proof narrative — both in the same file. Search for both dates when browsing.

---

### 2. Indian Censuses and Rolls (for Native, freedmen, and intermarried ancestors)
**Digitization: Indexed + Images (FamilySearch collection) / Browse-only (Dawes enrollment jackets)**

If your ancestor had any connection to the Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole), their freedmen, or intermarried non-Native citizens, these records are essential.

**FamilySearch Collection:**
- [Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432) — 567,890 records, 283,945 images. Includes tribal rolls and annual Indian census schedules.

**Digitized Volume (Browse-Only):**
- Image Group **005221389** — Dawes Commission enrollment jackets, 1898–1910. 176 images. **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** — must be browsed image-by-image with no search capability. These are the individual case files for each person enrolled on the Dawes Rolls, containing detailed family information, testimony, and sometimes photographs.

> **Quirk:** The Dawes Rolls (Final Rolls of Citizens and Freedmen of the Five Civilized Tribes) are the authoritative list determining allotment eligibility. Being on or off the rolls had profound legal consequences. Many families disputed their enrollment status — those records can be especially rich.

---

### 3. County Marriage Records
**Digitization: Indexed + Images**

- [Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789) — 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images. County-level marriage registers beginning in 1890 (when Oklahoma Territory was organized). This is the primary indexed marriage source for the Land Run era.

> **Quirk:** Marriages before county organization (April 1889–early 1890) may have no civil record. Church registers or territorial court filings are the substitute.

---

### 4. Mission and Church Records
**Digitization: Indexed + Images**

- [Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321) — 123,456 records, 61,728 images. Denominational congregations established in newly opened towns beginning in 1889; mission records predate civil settlement.

The FamilySearch Wiki notes (source: [Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)) that church records begin sporadically in 1889 as denominations established congregations. Coverage is uneven in the earliest years — do not assume a congregation that existed in 1895 kept registers back to 1889.

---

### 5. Federal and Territorial Census Records
**Digitization: Partially indexed (1900, 1910); physical/microfilm (1890 territorial)**

| Census | Coverage | Notes |
|--------|----------|-------|
| 1890 Federal | Largely destroyed by fire | **Exception: Oklahoma's 1890 special territorial census survives** at the Oklahoma Historical Society — one of the very few 1890 census records in the nation |
| 1890 County Tax Rolls | Physical/microfilm | Document early settlers; held at Oklahoma Historical Society and county courthouses |
| 1900 Federal | Oklahoma Territory + Indian Territory enumerated separately | Accessible via Ancestry.com |
| 1910 Federal | First enumeration as a state | Accessible via Ancestry.com |

> **Quirk:** The 1900 census enumerated **Oklahoma Territory** and **Indian Territory** as separate schedules. Knowing which territory your ancestor lived in determines which schedule to search — do not assume they are combined.

---

### 6. Territorial Court Records
**Digitization: Physical / microfilm — limited online access**

Territorial district court records (1890–1907) include civil and criminal cases, **probate records**, guardianship files, and **naturalization records**. Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record, so Oklahoma territorial courts are a significant naturalization source for arriving immigrants.

**Repositories:**
- **National Archives at Fort Worth, Texas** — primary repository for Oklahoma Territory district court records, per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))
- **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City) — additional territorial and early state court records

> **Quirk:** Naturalization records before September 27, 1906 are not centralized at NARA. Search territorial and county court records at Fort Worth and the Oklahoma State Archives before assuming no naturalization record exists.

---

### 7. Vital Records (Births and Deaths)
**Digitization: Coverage gap — specific dates not confirmed by FamilySearch Wiki tools**

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records returned only generic content during this survey — specific statewide registration start dates for Oklahoma could not be confirmed from tool results. Do not assume statewide registration existed during the territorial period (1890–1907). **Church records, cemetery inscriptions, and county court records are the primary substitutes for this period.**

Check the [Oklahoma State Department of Health — Vital Records](https://www.oklahoma.gov/health/birth-and-death-certificates.html) directly for access policy and earliest dates held.

---

### 8. Military Records
**Digitization: Partially online**

- **Fold3** — service and pension records for Oklahoma veterans; includes Spanish-American War (1898) era records relevant to this period: [fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)
- **National Archives (NARA)** — pension files, service records, and bounty land warrants: [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)

Many Land Run settlers were Civil War veterans drawing federal pensions — pension files can contain rich biographical data on origins, family, and prior residence.

---

### 9. Cemetery Records
- **Find A Grave** — [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) — user-contributed cemetery transcriptions and photographs. Coverage of small rural Oklahoma cemeteries from this period is uneven; verify transcriptions against original stones or sexton records.

---

### 10. Historical Newspapers
- **Newspapers.com** — [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) — territorial and early-state Oklahoma newspapers. Local papers from Guthrie, Kingfisher, Oklahoma City, and other Land Run towns published land notices, homestead proof announcements (legally required public notice), court filings, and community news.

> **Quirk:** Homestead "final proof" notices were required to be published in a local newspaper before a patent could be issued. Search territorial newspapers for your ancestor's name — these notices often include township/range descriptions and can confirm or correct a land office filing date.

---

## Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds for This Period |
|------------|-------------------------------|
| **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** | Territorial district court records, naturalizations, Indian Territory records |
| **NARA Washington, D.C.** | RG 49 GLO homestead case files, pension records |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (OKC) | 1890 special territorial census, county tax rolls, territorial newspapers |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** (OKC) | Territorial and early state court records, state agency records |
| **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents — free, searchable online |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed collections (land, marriages, Indian rolls, church records) + 2 digitized volumes |
| **Ancestry.com** | 1900 and 1910 federal census |
| **Fold3** | Military service and pension records |

---

## Tracing Origins — The Departure-State Strategy

The FamilySearch Wiki notes ([Oklahoma Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)) that many Land Run settlers came from **Kansas, Texas, Missouri**, and other neighboring states. Since families typically arrived with established records elsewhere, always trace the family in their **departure state** for the years before 1889:

- Kansas (the most common staging ground for the 1889 run)
- Texas (particularly for settlers entering from the south)
- Missouri, Arkansas, Tennessee (common origins for the 1893 Cherokee Strip run)

The homestead final proof file may name the state and county of prior residence — use this as your bridge back.

---

## Research Gaps and Notes

- **FamilySearch Wiki pages** for Oklahoma Vital Records, Land and Property, Church Records, Probate, Census, and Military Records all returned generic content during this survey — Oklahoma-specific guidance was not available from those pages. Check them directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy).
- **Volume_search returned only 2 digitized volumes** for this period — this is a small set and may not represent the full extent of digitized material. Physical microfilm at NARA Fort Worth, the Oklahoma Historical Society, and the Oklahoma State Archives likely holds substantially more.
- The **Dawes Commission enrollment jackets** (Image Group 005221389) must be browsed image-by-image — plan for hands-on browsing time if your research involves Indian Territory families.

| 1763–1780 | British West Florida | Mobile area and interior |
| 1780–1813 | Spanish West Florida (Mobile District) | Mobile area; interior still contested |
| **1798–1817** | **Mississippi Territory** | **The primary jurisdiction at 1800 for most of present-day Alabama** |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory | Eastern half of former Mississippi Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama | Counties begin creating their own records |

**The critical fact for research around 1800:** Most of present-day Alabama was organized under the **Mississippi Territory** (created 1798, covering both present Mississippi and Alabama). County-level Alabama record-keeping as we know it — marriages, probate, deeds — did not begin until 1809 or later, as counties were formally organized. For the Mobile area specifically, Spanish colonial records apply until 1813.

**A note on "Alabama" records:** FamilySearch's Alabama-labeled collections largely begin in 1809 at the earliest, because that is when county-level record-making began after statehood-era organization. For events before ~1809, you must search the Mississippi Territory and colonial-era collections below. These are one continuous research trail despite the different jurisdictional labels.

---

## Record Types Available for the Target Period (c. 1780–1819)

### 🗓️ Census and Population Lists

**The most important substitutes for a census at 1800.** No standard federal census covers Alabama residents as a distinct group until 1810 (when they appear within Mississippi Territory returns).

- **Mississippi Territory Territorial Censuses, 1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810** enumerated settlers in what is now Alabama. According to the FamilySearch Wiki ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)), these are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery. Physical/microfilm access; digitization status for these specific lists was not confirmed by the volume search (see Digitized Volumes section below).

- **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (FamilySearch collection [2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)) — 287,634 indexed records; starts 1810; no images in this collection. Covers the first federal census years touching Alabama.

- **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890"** (FamilySearch collection [1927171](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171)) — 198,340 indexed records; starts 1792; no images. Covers the Mississippi Territory period, which includes present-day Alabama.

> ⚠️ **Digitization gap:** The volume search returned **zero** digitized, browsable image volumes specifically tagged to Alabama in the 1780–1819 window. The compiled census substitutes above are **index-only** (no accompanying images). Browse-only image volumes for the territorial-era censuses do not appear to be available through FamilySearch's current digitized holdings for this period.

---

### 🏡 Land and Property Records

**The single most productive record type for this period.** Federal land grants and territorial-era land transactions are the richest surviving source for settlers in Alabama around 1800.

- **"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"** (FamilySearch collection [1919694](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694)) — 312,450 indexed records, 156,225 images. Starts 1798, covering the full Mississippi Territory period, including Alabama. This collection **does have images** and is the key early record set.

- **Bureau of Land Management – General Land Office (BLM GLO):** Federal land patents granted to original settlers in Alabama (a "public land state") are searchable at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov). Many of the earliest Alabama patents date from 1803 onward following the opening of land offices.

- **Spanish and British land grants (pre-1798):** For the Mobile area and southwestern Alabama, land grants under Spanish and British authority are documented in the colonial records (see below). The FamilySearch Wiki notes that Spanish records of the Mobile District include land grants held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, with copies at the **Library of Congress** ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).

- **County deed books (1809+):** As Alabama counties were organized from ~1809, deed books began. These are held at county courthouses and are being progressively digitized, but coverage for the very earliest years is uneven.

---

### ⚖️ Court and Probate Records

- **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (FamilySearch collection [1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764)) — 438,210 indexed records, 219,105 images. Begins 1809 as counties organized. **Has images.** For events before 1809, there are no Alabama county probate records because the counties did not yet exist.

- **"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"** (FamilySearch collection [1855293](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293)) — 245,670 indexed records, 122,835 images. Starts 1799; covers the territorial period when Mississippi Territory courts had jurisdiction over present-day Alabama. **Has images.** This is the primary court record source for the 1799–1809 gap.

- Territorial court records (Mississippi Territory courts sitting within present-day Alabama) are also held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History** and the **Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH)**.

---

### 💍 Marriage Records

- **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (FamilySearch collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)) — 612,345 indexed records, 306,172 images. Starts 1809. **Has images.** No formal marriage registers exist for the Alabama region before county organization.

- **Church registers** are the primary (sometimes only) source for marriages before 1809. See Church Records below.

---

### ⛪ Church Records

- **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** (FamilySearch collection [1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396)) — 156,789 indexed records, 78,394 images. Starts 1803. **Has images.** Early Baptist, Methodist, and Presbyterian congregations were the first organized Protestant churches in territorial Alabama.

- **"Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950"** (FamilySearch collection [2034891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891)) — 87,654 indexed records, 43,827 images. Starts 1800. **Has images.** Covers territorial-period church records from both sides of the Mississippi/Alabama divide.

- **Catholic sacramental registers (Mobile area):** The Catholic Church maintained registers in Mobile under French and Spanish rule. These are among the oldest surviving records for any Alabama community. Holdings are at the **Archdiocese of Mobile** and have been partially microfilmed; some are held at the **Mobile Municipal Archives** and the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France** (French colonial records), and the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain** (Spanish colonial records). The FamilySearch Wiki explicitly notes French colonial records are also microfilmed and available at the **Mobile Municipal Archives** ([Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)).

---

### 🪖 Military Records

- **War of 1812 and Creek War (1813–1814):** These conflicts fall just after the target window but are closely related. Service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants for men who served are held at the **National Archives (NARA)**, accessible via Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com)).

- **Territorial militia rolls (c. 1798–1817):** Militia lists for the Mississippi Territory period are among the territorial records at **ADAH** and **MDAH**. The wiki_search confirmed that militia rolls are part of the territorial record set at ADAH ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)). These are likely physical/microfilm holdings.

- **Revolutionary War records:** Many Alabama settlers were Revolutionary War veterans or their descendants who migrated from the Carolinas, Virginia, and Georgia. Pension and bounty land files for those veterans are at NARA (also on Fold3 and Ancestry).

---

### 📋 Tax Records

- Territorial-era tax lists are among the earliest substitute sources for Alabama families and were sometimes compiled annually. These are held at **ADAH** and have been partially published and indexed. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms that tax lists are part of the territorial record series ([Alabama Genealogy — Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)).

---

### 🌍 Colonial Records (pre-1798, primarily Mobile area)

These fall before the target window but are essential background for families with Mobile-area roots:

| Colonial Power | Period | Key Holdings |
|---|---|---|
| **French** | 1702–1763 | Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| **British** | 1763–1780 | Public Record Office, London (now The National Archives, Kew) |
| **Spanish** | 1780–1813 | Archivo General de Indias, Seville; copies at Library of Congress |

Source: [Alabama Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

These are **indexed with images**, not browse-only. |
| **Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810)** | Confirmed at ADAH (Montgomery); **not confirmed as digitized browse volumes** in FamilySearch's holdings. Physical or microfilm access likely required. |

**Bottom line:** For the pure territorial period (1798–1809), the surviving records with any FamilySearch digital presence are primarily the Mississippi Territory-labeled land and court collections, both of which are indexed (not browse-only). True "page through the register image by image" browsing opportunities for Alabama specifically around 1800 are very limited in FamilySearch's current holdings — the volume search returned nothing for this window. Researchers wanting the unindexed microfilm for territorial-era records should contact **ADAH** directly and check their [online catalog](https://www.archives.alabama.gov/).

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery** | Territorial censuses, militia rolls, tax lists, early county records, compiled indexes — the single most important repository for this period |
| **Mississippi Department of Archives and History (MDAH)** | Mississippi Territory court and land records that also covered present-day Alabama |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal land patents, military service and pension records |
| **BLM General Land Office** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Federal land patents, online and searchable |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Mobile city and Mobile County records; French colonial microfilm |
| **Archdiocese of Mobile** | Catholic sacramental registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) from the colonial era |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence (France)** | French colonial records for Louisiana and Mobile |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville (Spain)** | Spanish colonial records for Mobile District |
| **Library of Congress** | Copies of Spanish colonial records |

---

## Research Quirks and Cautions

1. **There are no Alabama county records before ~1809** — counties did not exist as administrative units. Don't search for "Baldwin County deed books" at 1800; search the Mississippi Territory records.

2. **Mississippi Territory collections also cover Alabama.** When searching FamilySearch's Mississippi-labeled territorial collections (land, court, church), these covered the whole territory including present-day Alabama. Search them even though the label says "Mississippi."

3. **The Mobile area is a different world.** Its records are in Spanish and French before 1813, held primarily in European archives and the Mobile Municipal Archives — not at ADAH. Factor in Spanish-language research skills.

4. **Tax lists are the best annual census substitute.** For the 1798–1810 window before the first federal census fully covers Alabama, territorial tax lists at ADAH are the closest thing to a year-by-year population listing.

5. **Adjoining states fed Alabama's early settlement.** Families who appear in Alabama around 1800 typically came from Georgia, the Carolinas, Virginia, or Tennessee. Searching originating states' records (especially Georgia land lotteries) often provides the family's earlier paper trail and fills gaps in the sparse territorial documentation.

6. **FamilySearch wiki pages for Alabama-specific topics (Vital Records, Land, Church, Probate, Census)** returned only generic content in this survey — not Alabama-specific guidance. For detailed Alabama research strategies, consult the [FamilySearch Alabama Genealogy Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy) and ADAH's research guides directly.

# Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide
### Irish Immigrant Coal Miners · 1860s–1890s
**Counties surveyed:** Schuylkill · Luzerne · Lackawanna · Carbon · Northumberland · Columbia

---

## Jurisdictional Context

**Schuylkill County** is the only coal county that resolved to a county-level standard place in the FamilySearch place tool (`Schuylkill, Pennsylvania, United States`). It was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties. Volume and external-link searches for the remaining five counties (Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, Columbia) resolved only to Pennsylvania state level; detailed volume data for those counties could not be retrieved at the county level in this session — a coverage gap to note.

**Critical jurisdictional split — Lackawanna County:** The FamilySearch coal-region wiki page refers to the Diocese of Scranton beginning post-1868, which aligns with the formation of Lackawanna County from Luzerne County in 1878. **Any record for a Lackawanna Valley ancestor (Scranton area) before 1878 will be filed under Luzerne County** — search Luzerne County records first for events in that window.

**Population growth, Schuylkill County** (from FamilySearch place data):

| Year | Population |
|------|-----------|
| 1860 | 89,510 |
| 1870 | 116,428 |
| 1880 | 129,974 |
| 1900 | 172,927 |

This rapid growth reflects the massive influx of Irish and other immigrant miners during the anthracite boom.

---

## ⭐ Coal-Region Specialized Indexes
*Source: [Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records)*

These indexes are unique to the anthracite field and sit alongside standard civil records. They are the most direct route to individual immigrant miners:

### 1. Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index, 1855–1898
Names approximately **41,000 colliery workers** across the lower anthracite field, drawn from company payroll books that survived a 1903 records consolidation. Each entry includes:
- **Occupation** (loader, breaker boy, mule driver, etc.)
- **Wage rate**
- **Parish of origin** where stated — invaluable for connecting a miner to an Irish townland

This is the most direct genealogical finding aid for immigrant miners whose names were indexed inconsistently in census records.

### 2. Company Payroll Indexes vs. Mine-Inspection Reports
The wiki specifically advises researchers to **distinguish between**:
- **Company payroll indexes** — name individual workers; use these first for tracing immigrants
- **Mine-inspection and accident reports** — organized by colliery, not by person; less useful as a personal name index but can confirm the specific colliery where an ancestor worked

### 3. Pennsylvania State Triennial Tax Assessments, from 1853
State assessors enumerated coal-region residents every three years beginning in 1853. Assessment ledgers list householder, real estate value, occupation, and **sometimes nativity** — making these a partial substitute for civil vital registration that Pennsylvania lacked during this period.

---

## Vital Records

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Pennsylvania Vital Records, Pennsylvania Genealogy, and all six county genealogy pages returned only a generic fallback in this tool environment — no Pennsylvania-specific registration dates were retrieved. This is a coverage gap; consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly for registration start dates.

**What is confirmed from the coal-region wiki:** Catholic church registers are the primary vital record source for Irish miners throughout the 1860s–1890s. Pennsylvania lacked statewide civil vital registration during this period (it did not begin until the early twentieth century based on standard historical record).

**FamilySearch digitized volume — Death Records:**
- Pennsylvania Death Records 1852–1968 (image group 008120442, 674 images) — **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable)

---

## Church Records — PRIORITY SOURCE FOR IRISH CATHOLICS

Catholic parishes in the coal region were established **between 1840 and 1870** specifically to serve Irish and Eastern European immigrant communities. Parish survival is confirmed by the wiki as generally good for this period.

**Diocesan custody:**
- **Diocese of Scranton** — holds baptismal registers for Lackawanna and Luzerne county parishes, **post-1868**
- **Diocese of Harrisburg** — holds registers for Schuylkill, Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia county parishes, **and for the entire region pre-1868**

**FamilySearch digitized volume (Schuylkill County):**
- Church Records 1842–1895 (image group 007936751, 187 images) — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable). Contains both English and German records.

---

## Census Records

Federal decennial censuses (1860, 1870, 1880, 1890, 1900) are the primary census sources. Note:
- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885)** record deaths in the year preceding each census — valuable before civil death registration existed
- The **1890 federal census is largely destroyed** (nationwide fire loss); no Pennsylvania-specific wiki guidance was returned for substitutes in this tool environment

# Vermont Pre-Statehood Locality Research Guide
**Period:** c. 1750–1791 (pre-statehood)
**Standardized place:** Vermont, United States
**FamilySearch place link:** https://www.familysearch.org/en/research/places/?text=Vermont&focusedId=46

---

## 1. Jurisdictional Context

Vermont has one of the most tangled pre-statehood jurisdictional histories in New England. Records for your ancestors may exist under **three different competing authorities**, and knowing which one applies to your ancestor's time and place is the prerequisite to any search.

**Phase 1 — New Hampshire Grants (c. 1749–1764)**
Governor Benning Wentworth of New Hampshire issued township grants across what is now Vermont, drawing in the first wave of settlers. New Hampshire's colonial courts held jurisdiction; records were generated in New Hampshire.

**Phase 2 — New York Dispute (1764–1777)**
A 1764 royal proclamation extended New York's boundary to the Connecticut River. New York asserted jurisdiction, declared New Hampshire grants void, and issued competing land patents. Families holding NH-grant titles faced ejectment suits in New York courts. The Green Mountain Boys (Ethan Allen and company) organized armed resistance. Records for Vermont settlers during this period can appear in **New York colonial or state archives** just as easily as in New England repositories — or in both simultaneously.

**Phase 3 — Republic of Vermont (1777–1791)**
Vermont declared independence in January 1777 and operated as a sovereign republic for fourteen years. It established its own government, confirmed or invalidated land titles, and built a county-court system as it went:

| County | Established |
|--------|-------------|
| Bennington | 1778 |
| Windham | 1779 |
| Windsor, Rutland, Orange | 1781 |
| Addison | 1785 |
| Chittenden | 1787 |

The **town** was the fundamental administrative and record-keeping unit throughout — more so than the county.

**Phase 4 — Statehood (March 4, 1791)**
Vermont became the 14th state. Later counties (Caledonia, Essex, Franklin, Grand Isle, Lamoille, Orleans, Washington) were not formed until after statehood.

> ⚠️ **Critical search implication:** An ancestor living in Vermont in the 1760s–1770s may have records in New Hampshire (NH grant documentation), New York (land dispute and ejectment files), *and* Vermont (once town government was established). Do not confine your search to Vermont archives alone.

---

## 2. What the FamilySearch Wiki Documents for Vermont

**Source:** FamilySearch Wiki — *Vermont Genealogy*, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy
*(All four `wiki_place_page` sections — home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips — returned this same page.)*

The FamilySearch Wiki documents **three items specifically** for pre-statehood Vermont research:

### ⭐ Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule
The Wiki calls this **"the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."** Prepared under New York colonial authority, it enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry contains:
- Grantee name
- Township grant date
- Acreage
- Disputed-claim status

If your ancestor was a land claimant in Vermont before 1771, this is the first place to look. It predates any Vermont civil registration system.

### Civil Vital Records
The Wiki states plainly: **statewide civil registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in 1857** — sixty-six years after statehood and well outside the pre-statehood window. Earlier **town clerk records** (some going back to the 1770s) survive, but unevenly. The Wiki directs researchers to **consult town clerk offices directly**. No statewide or FamilySearch-indexed vital records collection is documented for this period.

### Town Histories
19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) **"often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access,"** per the Wiki. These are a key substitute source for primary records that have not been digitized or that are held only in individual town offices.

### Coverage Gap — Vermont-Specific Record Type Pages

The *Vermont Genealogy* overview page is the only substantive Vermont-specific wiki content the tools returned.

---

## 3. Record Types for the Pre-Statehood Period

### A. Land and Property Records ⭐ PRIME SOURCE FOR THIS PERIOD

Land records are the **single most productive record class** for pre-statehood Vermont, for a simple reason: no civil vital registration existed, no federal census covers this period, and nearly every settler's presence in Vermont was documented through a land transaction.

| Record | What It Contains | Where Held |
|--------|-----------------|-----------|
| Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule | ~1,800 NH-grant grantees; name, township, acreage, disputed status | Vermont State Archives (VSARA) |
| New Hampshire colonial grants (Wentworth grants, 1749–1764) | Original NH township patents creating Vermont settlements | NH State Archives; printed in *NH State Papers* volumes |
| New York colonial land patents & court records (1764–1777) | NY-issued patents; ejectment suits against NH grantees | New York State Archives |
| Town proprietors' records (1760s–1791) | Proprietors' meeting minutes, lot draws, surveys, settler lists | Individual town clerks; Vermont State Archives |
| Town deed books | Deeds, mortgages, and land transfers recorded at town level | Town clerk offices; Vermont State Archives; FamilySearch Catalog |

> **Access note:** `collections_search` and `volume_search` tools were unavailable in this survey session, so no count of FamilySearch-digitized Vermont land volumes can be reported. Search the **FamilySearch Catalog** directly at familysearch.org/catalog under the specific Vermont town to find microfilmed deed books and proprietors' records.

---

### B. Vital Records — COVERAGE GAP for Pre-Statehood Period

As documented by the FamilySearch Wiki: **no statewide vital registration existed before 1857.** For pre-statehood births, marriages, and deaths, you must assemble evidence from substitute sources:

- **Town clerk records** — Some towns recorded vital events from the 1770s onward, but survival is uneven. Contact each town clerk directly.
- **Church records** — The primary substitute (see section C).
- **Gravestone inscriptions** — Supply death dates and sometimes ages.
- **Family bibles** — Not systematically indexed; look for them in manuscript collections at the Vermont Historical Society.
- **Town histories** — Often include vital-record abstracts transcribed from church registers (see section H).

No FamilySearch-indexed collection for Vermont pre-statehood vital records is documented in the wiki pages returned by this survey.

---

### C. Church Records

Church records — baptisms, marriages, burials — are the **primary substitute for civil vital registration** in this period.

**Denominations active in pre-statehood Vermont:**
- **Congregationalists** — The dominant denomination among migrants from Massachusetts and Connecticut
- **Baptists** — Growing rapidly from the 1770s onward; strong in many Vermont towns
- **Methodists** — Established circuits in Vermont in the 1780s
- **Presbyterians**
- **Quakers** — Present especially in Addison and Chittenden Counties
- **Anglicans/Episcopalians** — Smaller presence, often associated with Loyalist or Anglican-grant settlers

**Where records are held:**
- Individual surviving churches (many still active)
- Vermont State Archives
- Vermont Historical Society (vermonthistory.org)
- Congregational Library & Archives, Boston — holds New England Congregational registers
- Denominational archives (e.g., Baptist historical societies)

**Access:** No specific FamilySearch digitized collection for Vermont pre-statehood church records was documented by the available tools. The FamilySearch Wiki's *Vermont_Church_Records* page was not found in the wiki corpus. Search the FamilySearch Catalog under specific Vermont towns and denominations.

---

### D. Census Records — NOT AVAILABLE for Pre-Statehood Period

**Federal census:** The first federal census was taken in 1790. Vermont was not yet a state and was **not enumerated in 1790**. The first federal census that includes Vermont is **1800**. The Ancestry.com U.S. Federal Census Collection returned by the external links search for the 1750–1791 window is not applicable to pre-statehood Vermont research — it is noted here only to flag that the 1790 census cannot help you.

**Republic of Vermont census:** No Vermont republic-era census has been documented by the FamilySearch Wiki tools in this survey.

**Substitute:** Tax lists (see section F below) are the functional equivalent of a census for the pre-statehood period, documenting who lived where and what they owned.

---

### E. Probate Records

Vermont established county probate courts as it organized its counties during the Republic period. Probate records — wills, estate inventories, guardianship files, letters of administration — document property, family relationships, and named heirs.

**Probate jurisdiction during pre-statehood:**
Records would be filed in the probate court of the county in which the deceased resided at death. Since county formation was ongoing during this period (see the county formation table above), check when the relevant county was established — earlier estates may have been filed in the first available county court.

**Repository:** County probate courts (physically); Vermont State Archives holds copies of many series. The FamilySearch Wiki's *Vermont_Probate_Records* page was not found in the wiki corpus — search the FamilySearch Catalog directly for microfilmed or digitized Vermont probate volumes.

---

### F. Tax Lists and Assessment Records

Town **grand lists** (annual property tax assessment rolls) and **poll tax lists** (enumerating adult males) are critical substitutes for census evidence in the pre-statehood period.

- Grand lists document property ownership and values — placing a person in a town at a specific year
- Poll lists enumerate adult male residents, functioning as a de facto male-only population inventory
- Vermont towns were levying taxes from the early Republic period (late 1770s onward)
- The Republic of Vermont also collected state-level taxes

**Repository:** Vermont State Archives; individual town clerks; Vermont Historical Society manuscript collections.

---

### G. Military Records — Revolutionary War

The entire pre-statehood period coincides with the Revolutionary War (1775–1783) and its immediate aftermath. Vermont residents served in:
- **The Continental Army** (under New England regimental organizations)
- **Vermont militia units** (organized by the Republic of Vermont, 1777 onward)
- **The Green Mountain Boys** (irregular forces, pre-1777)

**Revolutionary War pension files** are among the richest genealogical sources for this period — applications often contain detailed biographical narratives including age, birthplace, marriage date and place, wife's name, children's names, and migration history.

| Resource | What It Contains | Access |
|----------|-----------------|--------|
| NARA (archives.gov) | Service records, pension files, bounty land warrants | Free finding aids; records on Fold3 / Ancestry (subscription) |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Digitized Revolutionary War service and pension records | Subscription; returned by FamilySearch external links search |
| *Rolls of Soldiers in the Revolutionary War* (State of Vermont) | Vermont-published compilation of VT soldiers | Vermont Historical Society; digitized on Archive.org |
| Vermont State Archives | Vermont militia records, Republic-era military papers | vsara.vermont.gov |

Both **NARA** (archives.gov) and **Fold3** (fold3.com) were returned by FamilySearch's external links search for Vermont in the 1750–1791 window.

---

### H. Town Histories and Published Genealogies

Specifically highlighted by the FamilySearch Wiki as a key access point: **19th-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) frequently reprint colonial-era proprietors' records** that are otherwise difficult to access, along with:
- Original proprietors' and settler lists
- Church register abstracts
- Family genealogies contributed by local residents
- Transcriptions of early town meeting records

**Access:**
- **Archive.org** (archive.org) — Many Vermont town histories are fully digitized and free to search
- **Vermont Historical Society** (vermonthistory.org) — Extensive collection; online catalog
- **Google Books** — Full-text searchable for many titles

---

### I. Cemetery Records

**Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) — returned by FamilySearch's external links search — indexes Vermont gravestone inscriptions and photographs. For pre-statehood deaths, gravestones may supply birth dates, death dates, ages, and occasionally spouse or parent names.

The **Vermont Old Cemetery Association** has conducted systematic gravestone surveys across the state; results are often deposited with the Vermont Historical Society or local historical societies.

---

### J. Newspapers

**Newspapers.com** (newspapers.com) was returned by FamilySearch's external links search. Pre-statehood Vermont newspaper coverage is thin: the first Vermont newspaper, the *Vermont Gazette* (Bennington), began in 1781; the *Vermont Journal* (Windsor) followed in 1783. Both began during the Republic period, not before it. Search for legal notices, land transactions, military notices, and obituaries.

**Chronicling America** (loc.gov/chroniclingamerica) — Library of Congress free newspaper database — may hold some of this early Vermont digitization.

---

## 4. Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | Holdings Relevant to Pre-Statehood Vermont | URL |
|-----------|------------------------------------------|-----|
| Vermont State Archives (VSARA) | Republic of Vermont records; county court records; town records deposited with state; 1771 Grant Survey Schedule | vsara.vermont.gov |
| Vermont Historical Society | Town histories, genealogies, newspapers, church record transcriptions, manuscripts | vermonthistory.org |
| Individual Town Clerks | Land records, proprietors' books, town meeting minutes, early vital records (holdings vary widely by town) | Contact each town directly |
| New Hampshire State Archives | Wentworth/NH colonial grants for Vermont townships | sos.nh.gov/archives |
| New York State Archives | NY colonial land patents; ejectment court records (1764–1777 period) | archives.nysed.gov |
| NARA | Revolutionary War service records, pension files, bounty land warrants | archives.gov |
| FamilySearch Catalog | Microfilmed Vermont town and county records | familysearch.org/catalog |
| Fold3 | Digitized Revolutionary War records | fold3.com (subscription) |
| Find A Grave | Vermont cemetery and gravestone records | findagrave.com (free) |
| Archive.org | Digitized Vermont town histories (free full text) | archive.org |

---

## 5. Key Quirks and Caveats

1. **Three jurisdictions, one ancestor.** Records may exist in New Hampshire, New York, *and* Vermont for the same individual, depending on when they arrived and what disputes they were involved in. Always check all three.

2. **No statehood = no 1790 census.** Vermont was not enumerated in 1790. The 1800 census is the earliest federal census for Vermont. Tax lists are the census substitute.

3. **Vital registration began in 1857**, per the FamilySearch Wiki — 66 years after statehood. No civil vital records exist for the pre-statehood period. Church records and town clerk records (where they survive) are the primary sources.

4. **Research by town, not by county or state.** Vermont's record-keeping was fundamentally town-based. A county-level search will miss the primary records. Identify the specific town before searching.

5. **The 1771 Grant Survey Schedule is the earliest name list.** If your ancestor was a landholder in Vermont before 1771, this is the starting point — approximately 1,800 grantees documented.

6. **Town histories reprint otherwise-inaccessible early records.** Per the FamilySearch Wiki, 19th-century published town histories are not just secondary sources — they are often the only accessible version of colonial-era proprietors' records.

7. **FamilySearch digitization coverage unknown.** `collections_search` and `volume_search` were unavailable in this survey. Query the FamilySearch Catalog directly at familysearch.org/catalog under specific Vermont towns and counties to assess what has been microfilmed or digitized and whether it is indexed or browse-only.

---

## 6. Recommended Research Sequence

1. **Pin the town.** Vermont record-keeping is town-based. No statewide index covers this period, so identify the specific town before searching anything else.
2. **Search the Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (at VSARA) if land ownership before 1777 is plausible.
3. **Contact the town clerk** for surviving land records, proprietors' books, and any early vital records.
4. **Search the FamilySearch Catalog** (familysearch.org/catalog) for that specific town and county.
5. **Search Revolutionary War pension files** at NARA / Fold3 — they are biography-rich and often contain spouse names, ages, children, and migration narratives.
6. **Consult 19th-century town histories** via Archive.org or the Vermont Historical Society.
7. **Check New Hampshire and New York archives** if the ancestor arrived before 1777 or was involved in land disputes.
8. **Search Find A Grave** for gravestone data supplying birth and death years.
9. **Search early Vermont newspapers** (Chronicling America; Newspapers.com) for legal notices, land announcements, and military listings from 1781 onward.
